events.text: A heaven-born child must be rolled into the Lotus Ledger before the first full moon. Ho Ran, a herald of the Jade Court's Rolls, arrives with a brush and a form for {npc}: a name given by the Court's rite carries standing; a name given at home carries only love.
events.arc: The Name in the Lotus Ledger

choices.text: Name {him} by the Court's rite

effects.log: Ho Ran dips the brush. The name settles into the Ledger with a sound like a lid closing, and the infant blinks at the gold of it.

choices.text: Name {him} at home, in the old way

mem.note: named me over a bowl of rain

effects.log: You whisper the name over a bowl of rain, and nobody writes it anywhere. Ho Ran folds the form with the stiffness of someone who will mention this later.

choices.text: Give two names: one for the Ledger, one for the house

effects.log: The Court gets its name and the house keeps another. The child, who answers to both, answers to neither when called across a courtyard.

events.text: On {npc}'s naming day the barge rails are hung with paper lanterns. Ho Ran reads the auspice from the child's first breath of mist and frowns: the stars over the Floating Isles lean toward a quarrel. A guest murmurs that an early name draws ill luck.
events.arc: The Name in the Lotus Ledger

choices.text: Ask Ho Ran to read it again, slowly

effects.log: The second reading is gentler: a quarrel, yes, but a short one, and a warm ending. Ho Ran dislikes being asked and says so.

choices.text: Light every lantern and feast anyway

effects.log: The feast runs past midnight. The child sleeps through the singing, and the stars, ignored, quarrel with no one.

choices.text: Lay a crane's feather in the cradle for luck

effects.log: The feather curls into the infant's fist and stays there. Whatever the stars meant, it will have to go through the feather first.

events.text: At eight, {npc} is summoned by the Court as a ledger-page, the first duty of a Court-named child. Ho Ran waits at the gate with a robe of white and gold sewn small. {npc} looks at you, then at the robe, and asks whether the name was a gift or a loan.
events.arc: The Name in the Lotus Ledger

choices.text: Tell the truth: it was a loan, for standing

mem.note: said my name was a loan, and meant it

effects.log: {npc} nods slowly, as one does at a sum that finally adds. The robe goes on, and the honesty stays with {him} longer than the robe.

choices.text: Say it was a gift, and bless the road

effects.log: You say gift. It is true in the way that matters. {npc} walks through the gate with a straight back and looks over {his} shoulder twice.

choices.text: Refuse the summons and take {him} home

mem.note: took me from the Court gate

effects.log: Ho Ran writes a note for the Warden. {npc} says nothing all the way home and holds your sleeve the entire time.

events.text: Ho Ran returns bearing the Warden's notice: {npc} is unrolled, and an unrolled child may not set foot on the White Stairs. {He} has watched the others climb for a week from the cloud-dock, and today asks what is wrong with {his} name.
events.arc: The Name in the Lotus Ledger

choices.text: Take {him} to be rolled, with the name {he} has

mem.note: had my name rolled at last

effects.log: The Ledger takes it without complaint after all. Ho Ran enters it with a sniff, and {npc} climbs the first step the same afternoon.

choices.text: Say the name was a gift to the house, not the Court

mem.note: kept my name for the house

effects.log: {npc} considers this very seriously. The name is not mended, but something between you is, and the Stairs can wait.

choices.text: Petition the Warden for an exemption

mem.note: got me a pass in my house name

ok.log: The Warden, charmed against better sense, grants a stair-pass in a house name. Ho Ran is appalled.

fail.log: The Warden refuses, with a lecture on the Rolls. {npc} hears every word from behind the door.

events.text: {npc} has been collecting mortal things for a year: a clay whistle, a bent copper coin, a painted fan that came up in a trader's cloud-barge. Tonight {he} asks you, plainly, to be let down to the red dust, just for a season, to see how the small folk live.
events.arc: A Child Who Wanted the Red Dust

choices.text: Say yes, with conditions

effects.log: You set rules: a season, a crane-letter every month, a cloak that will not tear. {npc} agrees to all of it too fast to have read it.

choices.text: Say no, and explain why

effects.log: You tell {him} of kin left below, and how an afternoon up here is a lifetime there. {npc} listens white-faced and does not argue, which is how you know it is not over.

choices.text: Say you will take {him} down yourself, one day

effects.log: {npc} lights up like a lamp. The one day becomes a promise in the child's ledger, and promises are collected.

events.text: Old Wen, keeper of the cloud-docks, takes you aside. {npc} has been seen at the dock every dusk, pestering the crane-handlers about the downward lanes. Old Wen has a soft heart and a loose tongue, and says only that cranes can be bribed with plums.
events.arc: A Child Who Wanted the Red Dust

choices.text: Thank Old Wen and watch the dock

effects.log: You watch from a pillar. {npc} feeds a crane a plum and whispers to it. The crane eats the plum and looks unmoved.

choices.text: Ask Old Wen to turn a blind eye on the child's side

mem.note: had a blind eye turned for me

effects.log: Old Wen smiles into the beard. The cranes at the dock learn a very slow way of taking off.

choices.text: Warn the crane-handlers off the plums

mem.note: had the dock closed to me

effects.log: The handlers promise, and each one pockets a plum on principle. {npc} finds other ways.

events.text: A crane-letter comes from the red dust in {npc}'s hand, scribbled on mulberry paper. {He} has met a lamp-seller's family in a river town, learned to haggle, and been given a nickname you are not to hear. {He} asks you to come down for the autumn lantern fair.
events.arc: A Child Who Wanted the Red Dust

choices.text: Go down to the fair

effects.log: The lantern fair is loud and sticky and poor. {npc} hands you a skewer and shows off the whole town, and you remember what the air smells like.

choices.text: Send a cloud-gift and a letter instead

mem.note: sent a box instead of coming

effects.log: The gift is a boxful of cloud-silk, which the river town cannot afford to wear. {npc} writes back, politely, to say thank you and come anyway.

events.text: {npc} has been sneaking off at night to the lowest edge of the Isle, and tonight the cloud-wall there is thin as muslin. You find {him} standing at it with a bundle on {his} back, looking down at a smudge of river light that is a town that does not know it is watched.
events.arc: A Child Who Wanted the Red Dust

choices.text: Stand beside {him} and look

mem.note: stood at the cloud-wall with me

effects.log: You look together for an hour. It is a bad hour, and a good one. By dawn {npc} puts the bundle down, still facing the town.

choices.text: Take the bundle and promise a descent

effects.log: You carry the bundle home yourself and promise a descent, in a year, with you. It is a heavier thing than the bundle.

choices.text: Close the thin cloud with a breath of qi

ok.log: You close the cloud-wall. {npc} is furious, then very quiet, then a good deal older.

fail.log: The cloud will not close for you tonight. {npc} watches your face as you fail, and learns something about elders.

events.text: Instructor Baek Jin keeps the lowest landing of the White Stairs, where heaven-born children spar before they are allowed to climb. {npc} has been practising a fortnight with a broom and will not say why. This morning Baek Jin sends word: a bout, at noon, against a child of the Thunder Gate House.
events.arc: The Child's First Spar on the White Stairs

choices.text: Drill {him} on footwork all morning

mem.note: drilled me before my first bout

effects.log: You drill the footwork until the broom is a blur. {npc} goes to the landing with sore calves and a clear head.

choices.text: Tell {him} to enjoy it and not to mind the result

effects.log: {npc} nods, unconvinced, and then, lighter, goes to eat a pastry. The nerves are still there, but they have somewhere to sit.

choices.text: Tell {him} to win, whatever it takes

effects.log: {npc} hears only the first half. The Thunder Gate child, by noon, is {his} whole world and nothing else is in it.

events.text: Baek Jin rings the landing bell. The Thunder Gate child, Sora, is a head taller and glares through a fringe of dyed lightning-thread. {npc} bows exactly as practised, and then, before the bout, says something low to Sora that makes the bigger child laugh and flinch.
events.arc: The Child's First Spar on the White Stairs

choices.text: Watch closely and shout the bell-count

mem.note: won my first spar with your count

ok.log: {npc} hears the count and times a clean sweep exactly on the third bell. Sora lands in a tangle of lightning-thread, astonished.

mem.note: lost my first spar on the Stairs

fail.log: {npc} loses the third bell to Sora's elbow and sits down hard. Baek Jin, impassively, rings the bout closed.

choices.text: Say nothing and let the bout be {his} own

ok.log: A gust off the cloud-sea lifts a loose thread across Sora's face at the right second. {npc} takes the opening and does not argue with luck.

fail.log: Sora is simply better. {npc} falls and rises and falls again, and at the last, grins through a split lip.

events.text: After a win on the White Stairs, {npc} is a small celebrity of the lowest landing. Sora's house sends a note asking for a rematch, politely, in lightning-thread ink, and Baek Jin quietly adds {npc} to the list for the next landing. {He} is already swaggering. You can see it from here.
events.arc: The Child's First Spar on the White Stairs

choices.text: Take the swagger down a notch, kindly

mem.note: told me about your first loss

effects.log: You tell {him} about the first time you lost. {npc} stops swaggering mid-step and starts listening, which is better.

choices.text: Let {him} enjoy it, for a day

effects.log: You let the day be golden. The next morning {npc} gets up before the bell, without being told, and goes down to the landing alone.

choices.text: Accept Sora's challenge for the next season

effects.log: A rematch it is. Two houses, two children and a good deal of lightning-thread ink. The Isle will be talking about it for weeks.

events.text: After the loss, {npc} stays at the landing long after the other children have gone. Baek Jin lets {him} stay. When you arrive, {he} is walking the bout again with a broom, step by step, correcting a stance against an empty space where Sora used to be.
events.arc: The Child's First Spar on the White Stairs

choices.text: Help {him} walk it through

effects.log: You take Sora's side of the bout, slowly. {npc} corrects you, then corrects the correction. The sun leaves the landing by degrees.

choices.text: Sit on the step and let {him} work

mem.note: sat with me at the landing

effects.log: You sit on the cold stone and say nothing for two hours. When {npc} is done, {he} sits beside you and says nothing for a while, too.

choices.text: Tell {him} the loss was a gift

effects.log: {npc} frowns, then grudgingly nods. Gifts of that kind are not unwrapped for years, but {he} has the box.

events.text: The Lady Yeon Soo of the Nine Clouds Palace has come in person, in a barge of lacquered silence, to see {npc}. Yeon Soo says {he} has the rare gift of listening to music no one is playing. The Palace would take {him} as a pupil, and keep {him}, for a century.
events.arc: A Child for the Five Powers

choices.text: Accept: a century is a day, above the clouds

effects.log: The papers are signed in cloud-silk. {npc} bows to the Lady, awkwardly, and gets a smile in return that is the first and last of the day.

choices.text: Decline: a century is too long to be apart

effects.log: Yeon Soo takes the refusal as a weather report. Yeon Soo leaves a single note on the table, in case the weather changes.

choices.text: Ask {npc}

effects.log: {npc} asks for a night, and an answer comes at dawn in the child's own hand. It is the first decision {he} has made that you did not steer, and the paper trembles.

events.text: A first letter comes from the Nine Clouds Palace, on paper so fine it is almost not there. {npc} writes with a new hand: precise, restrained, pleased. The Lady has taught {him} the first of the Palace's nine silences. The last line asks if you are well, and asks nothing else.
events.arc: A Child for the Five Powers

choices.text: Write back warmly, at length

effects.log: Four pages, with the news of the Isle. The reply, a month later, is a single page with a smudge on it, which you decide to read as a tear.

choices.text: Send a small gift of home: a pot of the old plum jam

mem.note: sent me home in a jar

effects.log: The jam crosses the Sea of Clouds in a crane's basket. The reply is three words: 'The jam arrived.' You read it twenty times.

choices.text: Ask the Lady if the child may visit

effects.log: The Lady agrees to a day in the autumn, as if conceding a border. You will count the weeks.

events.text: {npc} returns on the first autumn day, taller and quieter, wearing the Palace grey. At supper {he} corrects the way you hold your cup, gently and without malice, and then stops, horrified. The table falls silent. Something in the child has been rearranged.
events.arc: A Child for the Five Powers

choices.text: Laugh, and thank {him} for the lesson

mem.note: laughed when I corrected your cup

effects.log: You laugh, and after a moment so does {npc}. The silence lifts. {He} sits back, shoulders low for the first time that day.

choices.text: Ask what else the Palace has taught

mem.note: let me tell you what I learned

effects.log: {npc} tells you slowly, one thing at a time. Most are small. One is a cold thing about the Lady's own pupils and what becomes of them.

choices.text: Say you miss the child who didn't correct cups

mem.note: said you missed the old me

effects.log: {npc} flinches, then nods. 'Me too,' {he} says. It is not a reproach, and it is not a comfort, and it is true.

events.text: No Palace for {npc}. Instead, a spring morning finds {him} on the edge of the Palace's lawn, sitting with the pupils on the far side of the cloud-gap, listening to a lesson no one invited {him} to. Yeon Soo's eyes pass over {him} twice. {He} looks across at you, daring a reaction.
events.arc: A Child for the Five Powers

choices.text: Step onto the lawn and ask for {his} place

mem.note: asked the Lady for my bench

effects.log: The Lady hears you out with a tilt of the head. A place is found at the end of a bench, small and grudging, and entirely enough.

choices.text: Let {him} sit, and watch from the gap

mem.note: let me listen from the gap

effects.log: You stay on your side of the cloud-gap. {npc} learns more from the stolen lesson than from half a year at home.

choices.text: Call {him} home across the gap

mem.note: called me home from the music

effects.log: {npc} comes, slowly, looking back. The lesson goes on without {him}. At the door, {he} says only: 'It was good music.'

events.text: {npc} has gone into closed cultivation twice in a decade and come out the second time with a different weight to {his} step. At the tea-table you realise you can no longer read {his} qi: it is not hidden. It is simply higher than your sight.

choices.text: Say it aloud, and congratulate {him}

mem.note: named my rise aloud and was glad

effects.log: You say it. {npc} blinks, caught between pride and embarrassment, and pours your tea first.

choices.text: Pretend you noticed nothing

mem.note: pretended not to see my rise

effects.log: You pretend. {npc} lets you, politely, for two seasons. It is a worse kind of gift than the truth.

choices.text: Ask how the higher view looks

mem.note: asked what the higher view was like

effects.log: {npc} thinks about it as if it were an honest question, which it is. 'Cold,' {he} says. 'Quiet. And nobody there to tell about it.'

events.text: A guest of the House asks {npc}, in your hearing, who {he} learned from, and {npc} says your name. The guest looks at you with a new, interested face, and begins to ask how the House raised such a prodigy. You realise they are no longer asking about you.

choices.text: Take the credit gracefully

effects.log: You accept it, thinly. The guest goes away pleased. {npc} says nothing, and keeps the credit you took in a small drawer.

choices.text: Hand the credit back to {npc}

mem.note: gave me back my own rise

effects.log: 'It was never mine,' you say. 'I only kept the door.' The guest laughs. {npc} flushes, and does not look away.

choices.text: Say the House raised no one: {he} did it alone

effects.log: A blunt answer, quickly regretted by the guest. {npc} stares at the floor as if it had spoken.

events.text: {npc} comes to you with a vial of a rare pill and an offer. It is a breakthrough pill, the kind a House keeps one of in a thousand years. It would lift you a full realm. {He} says there is more, and no strain on the family. {He} holds it out, and it does not tremble.

choices.text: Accept it, and thank {him}

mem.note: gave you my pill and you took it

effects.log: You take it. The realm opens like a door you had forgotten was a door. {npc}, grinning, hovers to make sure you do not choke.

choices.text: Refuse: you will climb at your own pace

effects.log: {npc} sets the vial on the table and leaves it there for a week. The pill is still there. So is the offer. So is the pride.

choices.text: Take half and give half to the old gardener

mem.note: split my pill with the gardener

effects.log: You split the pill with the House's gardener, who is two realms from anything. {npc} pretends to be scandalised and is not.

events.text: A year on, {npc} stands at the edge of the clouds with a hand on your shoulder, and you finally notice that {he} has been standing beside you a long time, and that you were the one slowing. You are not behind. You are simply walking at the pace of the person you were.

choices.text: Walk on together at your own pace

effects.log: You walk the whole length of the terrace and back. At some point {npc} begins to match your step, not the other way round.

choices.text: Ask {him} to teach you the next form

effects.log: {npc} laughs aloud, then sobers. The lesson goes on until the lamps. It is the best you have been taught in a hundred years.

events.text: The pill sits on the table, in the same vial, a year later. {npc} has stopped mentioning it. {He} has also stopped dining at your table as often, and you notice, one evening, how large the empty seat is and how little you did with the years you could have shared.

choices.text: Go and find {him}, vial in hand

mem.note: came to find me with the vial

effects.log: You find {npc} in the garden, and say the pill was never the point. {He} says: 'No. It was the point.' And then, laughing: 'Eat it. I insist.'

choices.text: Keep your pace and let the seat stay empty

mem.note: left a seat empty between us

effects.log: The seat stays. You tell yourself it is dignity. {npc} sends a lamp-boy with a note: 'Door is always open.' You do not go.

events.text: {npc}, an elder of the Clan of the Nine Peaks and kin to your spouse, arrives unannounced with six attendants and a grievance: the House of the Silent Bell has begun tolling at the Peaks' own hour, an insult older than your marriage. They expect you to carry the protest.

choices.text: Carry the Peaks' protest to the Silent Bell

effects.log: {npc} is satisfied, and the Silent Bell is not. Your name is on the protest, in the Peaks' ink, from now on.

choices.text: Offer to mediate, quietly, before it spreads

effects.log: {npc} narrows an eye at the word quietly, but gives you a season. The attendants are less patient and say so on the stairs.

choices.text: Refuse to be anyone's messenger

effects.log: {npc} is cold to the bone, and the attendants cough. You have a quiet house, for now. Both houses quietly add your name to a different list.

events.text: The Silent Bell tolls day and night. The Peaks answer with drums on the White Stairs, and a haze of lacquer smoke drifts from both sides over the Sea of Clouds. Guests from each house, {npc} among them, keep passing through your halls, and each quietly asks which side your tea is brewed on.

choices.text: Serve tea in two pots, side by side

effects.log: The pots arrive at the table at the same moment. Both houses look suspicious. The tea, however, is good, and they drink it.

choices.text: Close the halls to both houses for a month

effects.log: A month of quiet. The bell and the drums go on outside the walls, as if at a distant war. You sleep well, and are resented.

choices.text: Take a night to listen at each house's gate

effects.log: You hear the feud from both sides in a single night, and learn it began over a borrowed lantern. It is both funnier and sadder than you thought.

events.text: Dame Eunseo of the Silent Bell comes in person, grey as a stormcloud, and says that the protest you carried has a flaw: it names the wrong hour. The Peaks have no standing to complain. Dame Eunseo says it kindly, and says it knowing {npc} is on the other side of the door.

choices.text: Argue the hour before both elders

ok.log: You argue the hour with a ledger in hand. Dame Eunseo is amused, {npc} is mortified, and the point goes to you both, which pleases nobody and ends the shouting.

fail.log: You get the hour wrong, in front of everyone. The Bell tolls twice, in what might be sympathy or might be mockery.

choices.text: Concede the hour and ask for peace

effects.log: Dame Eunseo accepts with a stiff nod. {npc} says you shamed the Peaks, and does not speak to you for a season.

events.text: You invite both houses to a tea on a neutral cloud, one the Jade Court's own cartographers leave unnamed. The Peaks arrive in grey and the Bell in silver. Dame Eunseo and {npc} take opposite ends of a long table, and neither is willing to be the first to pour.

choices.text: Pour for both, yourself

mem.note: poured the first cup for us

effects.log: You pour. Dame Eunseo accepts the cup like a conceded border. {npc} accepts like a conceded border from the other side. The feud takes a polite breath.

choices.text: Wait in silence until one of them breaks

effects.log: Eleven minutes of silence. Dame Eunseo breaks first, tartly, and the Peaks have won a point they did not want.

events.text: {npc} comes home from the Jade Court's autumn trials with the ribbon of second place and a face like an unlit lamp. That night you wake to find {him} at the mirror, speaking quietly to the glass. In it stands Jin Haeun, the one who won, smiling the exact smile of the trial hall.

choices.text: Sit down beside {him} and look in the mirror too

mem.note: sat with me at the mirror

effects.log: You look. There is only the two of you, and the glass full of a stranger. {npc} says: 'You cannot see {him}?' You say no. {He} breathes, once, as if given air.

choices.text: Cover the mirror and take {him} out onto the terrace

effects.log: The cloud-wind clears the head. The demon does not follow. It is still there in the morning, small and patient, in the polished brass of a kettle.

choices.text: Wake the household and call a Ministry healer

mem.note: called a healer on my shame

effects.log: A healer comes and calls it a minor distortion of the trial-heart. {npc} is more ashamed than relieved, and avoids your gaze for days.

events.text: The demon is a clever one. It does not lie. It recites the trial scores and the judges' faces and the exact stumble in the third form, which {npc} did make. Every true word is a nail. {He} turns to you at dinner and asks if you saw the stumble. You did.

choices.text: Say yes, and say what else you saw

mem.note: told me the truth that was left

effects.log: You say yes, and then the rest: the clean landing after, the spoken line that made a judge smile. The demon has told a third of the truth. You tell the other two.

choices.text: Say no, to spare {him}

effects.log: 'You are lying,' {npc} says quietly, and the demon grows two sizes at the table. A kindness that the demon can use is no kindness at all.

choices.text: Ask {him} what the stumble taught

effects.log: {npc} stares. Nobody has asked that. The demon, which only knows how to repeat, falters on the question and goes quiet for an hour.

events.text: Spring brings a new trial and a new date. {npc} says {he} will not go: the hall is the demon's house. But the Court has granted a rematch against Jin Haeun, an honour offered only once, and the demon has begun to whisper that you will be the first to be ashamed if {he} stays home.

choices.text: Go to the hall with {him}, in the gallery

mem.note: sat in the gallery for me

effects.log: You sit in the front row of the gallery, hands folded. {npc} sees you, steps onto the floor, and the demon, outnumbered, falls out of the room.

choices.text: Tell {him} to do as the heart says

mem.note: let me decide about the hall

effects.log: 'The heart says,' {npc} repeats, doubtfully. {He} goes. The rematch is clean and mostly {his} own, and you do not spoil it by watching.

choices.text: Tell {him} the Court can wait

effects.log: {npc} stays home. The Court does not wait, but it forgets, and a small silence settles into the house that nothing in it can quite fill.

events.text: Months after {npc} stopped dreaming of the mirror, a note arrives on cloud-silk from Jin Haeun: a polite, formal, startled letter. It says that on the morning of the trial, in the hall, {npc} bowed as no one had bowed before, and Haeun has not been able to forget the bow. Does {npc} wish to meet?

choices.text: Tell {npc} and let {him} choose

mem.note: let me answer the rival myself

effects.log: {npc} reads the letter three times and says yes, and then no, and then yes. The meeting is brief and moving, and the demon is, finally, someone's name.

choices.text: Hold the letter a day, then give it over

mem.note: held a letter for a day

effects.log: You hold it a day to see how {he} sleeps. Then you give it over, and say why. {npc} frowns, forgives you, and replies in the morning.

events.text: The demon fades in no dramatic way. {npc} merely notices, one morning, that the mirror is only a mirror. {He} sits in front of it a long time, then lights a stick of incense, tilts it to the empty glass, and says thank you to something no one else will ever see.

choices.text: Light a second stick beside {his}

effects.log: Two thin lines of smoke rise together. {npc} says nothing, and leans on your shoulder, and the mirror is only a mirror.

choices.text: Leave {him} to it, and put the kettle on

mem.note: put the kettle on after the mirror

effects.log: When {npc} comes through, the kettle is just starting to sing. The gift is made of something very ordinary, and very exact.

events.text: A cloud-barge you do not recognise ties up at your dock, and from it steps {npc}, a sibling of the old house whom you have not spoken to in three centuries, since the quarrel over the grotto deed. {He} stands very straight on the planks, a bundle in one hand, and does not say why {he} has come.

choices.text: Greet {him} by name and take the bundle

mem.note: took my bundle without a question

effects.log: 'It's you,' {npc} says, and a century of armour comes off {his} shoulders at once. The bundle is heavy with something you cannot guess.

choices.text: Receive {him} formally, as a visitor of rank

effects.log: You greet {him} as a stranger of standing. {npc} answers in kind, to the letter. It is possible to freeze a dock with manners.

choices.text: Ask first why {he} has come

effects.log: {npc} flinches, as if the question was the first blow in a fight. 'I am old,' {he} says, 'and the grotto is not worth it.' It is a beginning.

events.text: The first supper is quiet. Neither of you mentions the grotto deed. The talk is of cranes and the price of plums, and across the table {npc} turns the spoon over and over in {his} hand, the way {he} did as a child when about to confess to the broken lantern.

choices.text: Mention the grotto deed first

effects.log: You say it plainly. {npc} lets the spoon fall, and the pause that follows lasts an age. 'I forged the second page,' {he} says. 'I am sorry.'

choices.text: Wait for {him} to speak

effects.log: The spoon turns. Turns. 'The plums are very good,' {npc} says. You agree, and the supper ends there, and both of you lie awake.

choices.text: Pass the plums, and the subject

effects.log: You pass the plums. {npc} takes one with a small, lost bow, and the two of you finish the meal in a courteous, poisonous calm.

events.text: In the morning {npc} unwraps the bundle on the dock: a lacquer box, and in it the original grotto deed, the first page and the second, side by side. It was never lost. {He} has kept both for three hundred years, and tried to burn each, and could not. {He} pushes the box across the planks.

choices.text: Burn them together, with {him}

effects.log: You carry the box to the brazier. The deed burns in a clean yellow flame, and {npc} watches it with an expression of terrible, unburdened shock.

choices.text: Keep the deed, and the grotto, and say so

effects.log: You take the first page. {npc} takes the second. You agree to share the grotto for a season and see what the walls say.

choices.text: Press {him} on why now

mem.note: pressed me for the real reason

effects.log: 'Because I am old,' {npc} says. It is not the whole answer, and you can hear that it is not, and say so. {He} does not reply, but does not leave.

events.text: {npc} stays three days and takes the barge away on the fourth without saying goodbye. A letter follows, a month later, in a stiff, hurried hand: 'I should not have come. I could not have stayed. Thank you for the plums.' The grotto deed is not mentioned, and not forgotten. It will not be answered soon.

choices.text: Write back at once, and invite {him} again

effects.log: You write four pages and send them with the first crane. The answer takes a decade. It is warmer than the letter, and shorter, and kept.

choices.text: Let the silence stand a while longer

effects.log: You do not write. The barge goes on being absent. Some silences, once fed, grow their own gardens, and you find it hard to weed this one.

events.text: A crane lands on your sill in the dusk with a mulberry-paper letter in its beak, written by a stranger's hand in a village below: {npc}, a great-grand-niece of yours, the last who knows your name, lies dying of a winter fever. By your own reckoning it was a pleasant spring afternoon since you saw the first of the line.

choices.text: Take the next crane down at once

effects.log: You mount the crane before the letter is finished. The wind rips the paper from your hand and spreads it over the clouds like torn blossom.

choices.text: Send a Ministry healer ahead, and follow when you can

effects.log: The healer leaves at dawn with a vial of Mid-grade cloud-tonic. You gather your things slowly. Something in you is already a day behind.

choices.text: Stay: it is the way of mortals, and you cannot change it

effects.log: You write a reply, a long one, and give it to the crane. Then you sit at the sill all night, and the paper goes down alone.

events.text: Below, the red dust smells of wet straw and woodsmoke. The village remembers a legend of an immortal kinsman, and has put a small lamp in the eaves of {npc}'s house against the day you come. A neighbour woman, red-eyed, runs to meet you with the news you were afraid to hear, or not.

choices.text: Ask to be taken to {npc} at once

mem.note: came in through the low door

effects.log: The neighbour leads you through a low door. In the shadow of a bed, a very small old face turns on a pillow, and a hand rises like a leaf from a branch.

choices.text: Ask the neighbour what {npc} has said of you

mem.note: set a bowl by the door for you

effects.log: 'That you would come,' the neighbour says. 'Every spring, {he} set a bowl by the door.' You find the bowl on the doorstep, and it is wet.

events.text: {npc} has only a few hours. {He} holds your wrist with surprising strength and asks whether the Isles are as beautiful as the legends. You have a hundred answers, and none is true enough. The lamp in the eaves gutters in the draught, and your kin watches your face for the lie.

choices.text: Describe the Isles, simply

mem.note: told me what the Isles are like

effects.log: You tell {him} of a morning on the White Stairs, and the cranes, and the smell of cloud. {He} smiles at the roof, and says, 'Like a tea of rain.' It is close enough.

choices.text: Offer to carry {him} up, at the cost of {his} mortal span

mem.note: offered me the clouds and I refused

effects.log: You can lift {him} through the clouds in a stolen ascension. {He} laughs weakly: 'The red dust is where my people are.' {He} will not go, and forgives you the offer.

choices.text: Sit and say nothing, and hold {his} hand

mem.note: held my hand to the end

effects.log: You hold {his} hand. It cools a degree an hour. The lamp in the eaves burns steady, then dim, then out. You hold on a while after it.

events.text: The healer you sent comes back up the lane at dawn with the vial unopened. The healer did not reach {npc} in time. In the empty bed lies the bowl set out each spring for you, and a letter in a tiny script, left under it, that begins: 'In case you came late. I understood.'

choices.text: Read the letter, and light the lamp in the eaves

effects.log: You read it standing in the doorway. Then you carry the small lamp to the grave and set it down, and it burns all night against a wind that is not there.

choices.text: Tend the grave for a season before going home

effects.log: You stay a season, mend the roof, plant plums at the grave. The village is more pleased with the plums than the immortal.

events.text: {npc} stands in the door of your study with clenched hands and says it in one breath: {he} loves Han Seol, a pupil of the Demon Realm's far embassy, and means to marry. Every one of the five powers frowns on such a match. {He} is not asking for permission. {He} wants to know whether you will stay in the room.

choices.text: Stay in the room and hear the whole story

mem.note: stayed in the room for my story

effects.log: You stay. It takes the evening. {npc} speaks for the first time in decades without picking words, and by the end you are crying, which you do not mention.

choices.text: Say it cannot be, and give the reasons

effects.log: You give the reasons of the Court, in order. {npc} listens to every one, nods at each, and leaves without a word. You hear the door of {his} room very clearly.

choices.text: Ask to meet Han Seol before deciding

effects.log: {npc} looks surprised and then terrified. 'It is not a test,' you say. 'It is a supper.' {He} nods, and does not stop touching the hem of {his} sleeve.

events.text: A notice arrives from Minister Gwon Do-yun of the Celestial Ministries, on the Court's lilac paper: an informal inquiry into a cross-power attachment on an Isle under his watch. It is a courtesy. It is also a net. The Minister is fond of you, and has sent his regards in the last line.

choices.text: Answer with a careful, empty letter

effects.log: You write a letter that says nothing in four pages. The Minister replies with a kind two lines. The net stays loose, for now.

choices.text: Visit the Minister in person with a gift

mem.note: went to the Minister for me

effects.log: He receives you with tea and no illusions. 'Nothing will be recorded,' he says, 'until someone makes it a matter of record.' You leave with a warning wrapped in a courtesy.

choices.text: Tell {npc} about the notice

mem.note: told me the truth about the notice

effects.log: {npc} goes pale, then very still. 'Then we will not hide,' {he} says. You are proud and appalled at once, which, you understand, is what being a parent is.

events.text: The two of them are at your gate by night, with a bundle each. Han Seol, grave and young, bows to the doorpost and says that they have not come to take {npc} from the house, but to ask whether the house will let them be seen together in it. The Demon Realm sent no blessing. They ask for yours.

choices.text: Give your blessing aloud, in the courtyard

effects.log: You give it, in front of the doorpost and the lamps and the neighbours. Han Seol bows to the ground. {npc} grips {his} hand so hard that it will be bruised in the morning.

choices.text: Give them a season to prove it to the Court

effects.log: A season. A condition. They accept. They are a team already, you see, from the way they say yes in the same breath.

choices.text: Refuse, and bar the gate

effects.log: You bar the gate. It is a matter of principle and a matter of fear. In the dawn the bundle is still at the foot of the gate, and {npc} is not.

events.text: A letter from {npc}, no return address, on rough paper from somewhere low. {He} has left the Isles, with Han Seol, to a place where no power keeps a ledger. {He} writes that {he} is well, that {he} is not angry, and that there is a lamp in the window if you ever come down the long way.

choices.text: Write back, with the name of a crane-keeper who will carry post

mem.note: sent me a line from home

effects.log: You write the keeper's name and a short line: 'Whatever else you are, you are mine.' The line goes out on the evening cloud.

choices.text: Keep the letter and tell no one

mem.note: kept my letter in a drawer

effects.log: You keep it in a drawer, among other things, and visit the drawer more often than you admit. The Minister never asks, and the Isle does not know.

events.text: War is declared between the Jade Void Sect and the Star Sea Pavilion, and the house that bred {npc} calls its banners for the Void. Your own isle's Rolls pledge, formally, to the Pavilion. For the first time in your marriage, you and {him} are on opposite sides of a document.

choices.text: Stand with {npc}'s house, and write to the Void

effects.log: You write the pledge on your best paper. {npc} reads it twice and says nothing, and takes your hand in a way that is both thanks and bereavement.

choices.text: Stand with your isle and its Rolls

effects.log: You sign the Pavilion's Roll. {npc} watches from the doorway. 'It is only paper,' {he} says, and goes inside, and the door is not slammed.

choices.text: Sign nothing and declare the household neutral

effects.log: The household is neutral by decree. Both powers write to ask what that means. You compose a long, evasive answer, which pleases only the cat.

events.text: The first blockade comes down on the cloud-lanes. Stocks run thin at the dock. A Void barge and a Pavilion barge sit across from each other within sight of your terrace, silent, hung with pennants. On your table, {npc} spreads a map and says, very quietly, 'We can still choose how this goes.'

choices.text: Propose a household truce: no soldiers past the gate

mem.note: made a truce for our house

effects.log: A rule: no banner past the gate, no talk of the war over tea. It holds for most of a year, and it is the hardest piece of statecraft you have ever done.

choices.text: Argue your side hard, and let the house rage

effects.log: You argue until the lamps gutter. {npc} argues back. It is the best conversation you have had in a century, and the worst.

choices.text: Go out to the barges and talk to the pilots

effects.log: You talk to the pilots. They are tired boys with tea-flasks and sisters at home. The war becomes briefly, uncomfortably, small.

events.text: The war's turn comes in the autumn. The Void's flagship is struck and drifts towards your isle with a burning mast. {npc}, whose cousin is aboard, runs to the dock. The Pavilion's pickets have orders to turn it back by qi. The two of you are standing where you cannot be both loyal and decent.

choices.text: Hold the pickets with your own qi while the cousin lands

mem.note: saved my cousin from the mast

ok.log: The pickets stand down, startled. The cousin is lifted off the burning mast onto the dock, and {npc} laughs and sobs together and holds your sleeve.

fail.log: The pickets hold. The flagship burns out over the Sea of Clouds. {npc} does not blame you aloud, and does not look at you for a week.

choices.text: Order the pickets to turn it back, as the Roll requires

effects.log: The flagship drifts away on the wind, burning. {npc} stands motionless on the dock. 'You were within the law,' {he} says. It is the worst thing it could have been.

events.text: Peace comes by treaty on the first snow. The two powers sign on a cloud in the middle of the sea, and the powers' clerks go home to write up their gains. In your house, the war is not so tidily done. The truce rule is still on the wall, and {npc} is standing in front of it with a brush.

choices.text: Hand {him} the brush

effects.log: {npc} crosses out the word truce and writes, under it, in careful brush: 'Home.' The wall is repainted. The rule is the house's name from then on.

choices.text: Say the truce can stay a while, just in case

mem.note: left the truce on the wall

effects.log: The wall keeps its rule. A crack of old fear shows in the plaster beside it, and takes years to fill.

events.text: Peace comes by treaty on the first snow, signed on a cloud in the middle of the sea. In your house nothing is signed. You and {npc} sit across the table and find that the argument you had was the last honest thing either of you said, and neither can remember how it ended.

choices.text: Ask {him} to finish it, now, in peace

effects.log: It takes an evening. At the end {npc} concedes a point, and you concede two, and the lamp is lit again in a room that had forgotten it.

choices.text: Let it lie, and call it a draw

effects.log: A draw. The war is over and the house is quieter than it was. Years later you both still wonder who was right.

events.text: At the Ministries' root-test, {npc} lays a palm on the white jade and nothing happens at all. No colour, no pulse. The tester, a patient old woman named Pyo, says very gently that Pyo has seen it four times in a thousand years: a heaven-born child with no spirit-root. {npc} looks at the jade and not at you.

choices.text: Take {him} home and say it changes nothing

effects.log: You say it. It is true in the way that matters and false in every way that will be tested. {npc} nods and sleeps badly.

choices.text: Ask Madam Pyo what could be done

effects.log: Pyo names a cure, a rare and costly one, with a promise that it fails more than it works. {npc}'s hands move to hide in {his} sleeves.

choices.text: Say nothing, and hold {his} hand

mem.note: held my hand at the jade

effects.log: You hold it all the way down the White Stairs. Neither of you says a word, and at the bottom {npc} lets out a long, shaky breath.

events.text: Word travels fast on the Floating Isles. The next season, children of the neighbouring houses start calling {npc} the Empty Bowl, and the name is one of those that stick. {He} stops going down to the cloud-dock. When you ask, {he} says {he} is busy. {He} has never been busy in {his} life.

choices.text: Take {him} on a long walk and say nothing about it

mem.note: walked and talked of plums with me

effects.log: You walk the whole length of the Isle with {him} and talk about plums. Near the end {npc} says: 'They called me the Empty Bowl.' You say a bowl holds things. It is a start.

choices.text: Find the children and have a word

effects.log: You find them, and the word is short. The nickname goes out of use at once, in front of you, and a good deal more bitterly behind your back.

choices.text: Give {him} a task in the house: the lamps

effects.log: You put {npc} in charge of the household's lamps. It is a small trust and a real one. {He} trims them all that night with an exactness that is almost fierce.

events.text: Madam Pyo's cure turns out to be a year of daily bitter tonics, a month on a snow-peak, and the sacrifice of a cultivated treasure of the house to the Ministries' alchemists. {npc} says yes before you finish the list. The tonic is brewed that evening, and {he} drinks it in one go.

choices.text: Give the treasure and see it through

mem.note: gave the treasure for my root

effects.log: The treasure goes into the alchemists' furnace. The year is hard and the month harder. At the end the jade flickers, once, faintly green, and {npc} weeps in the Ministry courtyard.

choices.text: Hold back the treasure, try the tonics alone

effects.log: The tonics alone are bitter and less. After half a year there is a faint stirring, enough for a candle's worth of qi. {npc} is grateful, and aware of what you did not give.

events.text: {npc} has taken up the craft of lamp-making, starting with the household lamps and moving on to the Isle's. The lamps are good. They are better than good: each one burns a particular colour of flame that has no cultivation behind it, only patience. A Ministry clerk asks to buy ten for the Court.

choices.text: Accept the order on {npc}'s behalf

mem.note: sold my lamps to the Court

effects.log: The lamps go to the Court in a barge lined with straw. {npc} is paid in spirit stones and a bow, and stands in the dock the whole day with a faint, dazed smile.

choices.text: Let {npc} answer the clerk

effects.log: {npc} answers the clerk with a polite refusal, and a counter-offer, and a pair of lamps for the clerk's own desk. The clerk leaves charmed, and with a lamp.

choices.text: Tell the clerk the lamps are not for sale

effects.log: The clerk shrugs and goes. {npc} comes out of the workshop a moment later. 'Why?' {he} asks. Because they are yours, you say. It is not the right answer.

events.text: {npc} has been summoned to sit the Jade Court's Examination of Nine Questions, which opens a seat in the Rolls to anyone who answers seven. A clerk named Mun, who runs a quiet trade on the stair, offers you a scroll with the answers to the last three, for a favour to be named later.

choices.text: Refuse the scroll and send the clerk away

effects.log: Mun bows without offence and withdraws. The offer has a way of floating back, though, like a feather on a stairwell.

choices.text: Take the scroll and hide it in the cradle-chest

effects.log: The scroll goes into the chest under a layer of silk. You tell yourself you will decide in the morning. You will not sleep until then.

choices.text: Tell {npc} about the offer and let {him} decide

mem.note: let me decide about the scroll

effects.log: {npc} listens, goes grey, and says: 'I wish you hadn't told me.' Then, after an hour: 'No. But thank you for the trust.'

events.text: Examination morning. The hall of the Rolls is white, high and echoing, with the Nine Questions hung on nine silk banners. {npc} sits at a low desk among two hundred others. The moment the first banner is lowered, the room goes absolutely silent but for the soft hiss of ink on jade.

choices.text: Wait outside and hope

mem.note: sat the nine and got seven

ok.log: The doors open at dusk. {npc} comes out unsmiling but upright, and holds up seven fingers. 'Seven,' {he} says. 'Exactly seven.' You laugh until you cry.

mem.note: sat the nine and got six

fail.log: The doors open at dusk. {npc} walks past you and does not stop. Six. A single question short, and a long walk home.

choices.text: Wait outside and coach {him} by the light of memory

ok.log: Your memory of the Rolls turns out to be sharper than you thought. The hours go by like a prayer, and {npc} comes out knowing it went well.

fail.log: You tell {him} the wrong order of the sixth question's three clauses. It costs the seat by a hair.

events.text: The Rolls offer {npc} a seat as an under-clerk of the Lotus Ledger, the smallest chair in the Court, with a window onto the mist and a view of the brazier where discarded names are burnt. {He} accepts at once, and then lies awake wondering what it will cost.

choices.text: Tell {him} the seat is a door, not a cage

mem.note: told me the seat was a door

effects.log: You say it, and you mean it. {npc} nods slowly, and takes up the brush the next morning, and writes the first name very carefully.

choices.text: Warn {him} about the Court's politics

mem.note: warned me what the Court eats

effects.log: You give a careful, honest account of how the Court eats the young. {npc} listens like a student of an unwelcome science, and writes down a few of the names.

choices.text: Tell {him} to hold the seat for ten years and then see

effects.log: A ten-year plan. {npc} grins. 'The cleverest thing I have heard in a decade,' {he} says. 'Why is it so dull?'

events.text: Mun is back on the stair, bowing, with a very small, very polite smile. The favour has been named. A certain scroll in your chest, Mun says, could be quietly returned to the Court's cellars, if {npc}'s name were found among the seventy who 'passed' this year. Which, in strict honesty, it was not.

choices.text: Burn the scroll and report Mun yourself

mem.note: burned my seat for the principle

effects.log: You burn the scroll in the hall brazier and tell the Keeper of the Ledger everything. Mun leaves, in tears. {npc} is struck from the seat, and will never forgive the principle.

choices.text: Pay the favour and let the matter lie

mem.note: bought my seat through a clerk

effects.log: You pay in a small, unmentionable coin of influence. The scroll is returned. {npc} gets the seat. Both of you will know exactly how, for a long time.

choices.text: Tell {npc} everything and let {him} choose

mem.note: chose to burn the scroll with me

effects.log: {npc} listens with a still face. 'Burn it,' {he} says. The scroll burns. {He} sits the examination again next year, honestly, and it is the most proud you have ever been.

events.text: The failed child spends a month at the cloud-dock, throwing pebbles into the mist. When you come to fetch {him}, {npc} says: 'Six. I had six. Do you know how many I would have had if you'd bought the scroll?' {He} is not angry. {He} is wondering.

choices.text: Say you would never have bought it

mem.note: said you would not have bought the scroll

effects.log: 'I know,' {npc} says. 'I am glad.' It is the first time all week {he} has met your eyes.

choices.text: Tell {him} to sit again next year

mem.note: told me to sit it again

effects.log: {npc} sits again the next year, and gets eight. The fourth question, which {he} knew all along, cost {him} the first time.

events.text: The household is short of one lamp-boy's dinner every night, and {npc} is suspiciously cheerful. Following the crumbs you find a cloud-fox cub in the linen chest, no bigger than a loaf, curled on a nest of your silk. It looks at you with its pale eyes. Spirit-beasts of the clouds must be registered with the Ministries.
events.arc: The Cloud-Fox in the Linen Chest

choices.text: Keep the secret for now

effects.log: You close the chest quietly and say nothing. The cub's eyes follow you out. That night, {npc} leaves an extra rice-ball on the sill and thinks you did not see.

choices.text: Register the cub with the Ministries, and take {npc}

effects.log: You take {npc} and the cub down to the Ministries' beast-clerk, who writes it up with a flourish. The cub bites the quill. The clerk is delighted.

choices.text: Tell {npc} the cub must go back to the cloud-meadows

mem.note: said my fox had to go

effects.log: {npc} says nothing, and then says everything. The cub will not leave the chest. You are asked, with great dignity, to reconsider.

events.text: Officer Do of the Ministries' beast-watch arrives with a lantern and a ledger. A cub of the cloud-fox kind, Do says, has been smelled on the Isle, and unregistered ones are confiscated. He has the manners of a man who has confiscated many things and been spat at by most of them.
events.arc: The Cloud-Fox in the Linen Chest

choices.text: Charm Officer Do with tea

mem.note: got the officer to look away

ok.log: Do accepts the tea and a plate of rice-cake. The cub, hearing his voice, sneezes in its sleep. 'I am deaf in the left ear,' says Do, and eats another cake.

mem.note: lost my fox to the officer

fail.log: Do accepts the tea and is unmoved. Do goes to the chest as if guided by a rope. The cub is taken in a basket, and {npc} watches the basket go.

choices.text: Tell him the truth and ask for a licence

mem.note: asked for a licence for my fox

effects.log: Do considers this a very long moment. 'Honesty is not on my list,' says Do. 'Fill in this form.' It is eleven pages, and there is a space for the cub's paw-print.

events.text: The licensed cub, named Biscuit by the household and Moon-Under-the-Stairs by its mother, follows {npc} everywhere on the Isle, and has learned to ride the cloud-lift on {his} shoulder. A neighbouring House sends a polite note: its own heir has been bitten, and would like words.
events.arc: The Cloud-Fox in the Linen Chest

choices.text: Apologise with a gift and a rule for the cub

mem.note: made a rule for my fox

effects.log: The apology works. The rule, which is that Biscuit may not bite anyone below the knee, is written in red on the cub's basket and ignored by all parties.

choices.text: Ask the neighbour whether the heir provoked it

effects.log: The heir did. The neighbour goes slightly pink, and the matter dissolves into a very polite shared silence.

events.text: The cub is grown, and its mother's kind comes to the Isle in a fog, a whole family of them, to fetch it home to the cloud-meadows. They stand in the courtyard with their tails low. {npc} sits down on the paving with the great fox-cub and cries, without any dignity at all.
events.arc: The Cloud-Fox in the Linen Chest

choices.text: Let the fox go home, and go with {him} to the meadow edge

mem.note: walked my fox to the meadow

effects.log: You walk the fox to the meadow edge. It stops at the last stone, looks back once, and is gone in the fog. {npc} says nothing until the supper.

choices.text: Ask the foxes if the cub may visit

mem.note: asked the foxes for a visit

effects.log: The elder fox considers for a long time. The cub may come on the first mist of every spring. {npc} wipes {his} face on a sleeve and says, 'That is something.'

events.text: Without Biscuit, the house has a hole the exact shape of one small fox. {npc} walks by the linen chest and does not look in. A small basket with a bite-mark in the handle sits in the corner of the room, where {he} left it, and you are not sure whether to move it or leave it where it is.
events.arc: The Cloud-Fox in the Linen Chest

choices.text: Leave the basket where it is

effects.log: You leave it. For years the basket sits there in the corner, and {npc} gradually learns to see it without flinching.

choices.text: Offer {him} another animal, a cloud-hare perhaps

effects.log: 'Not a replacement,' {npc} says gently. 'I'll know when it's time.' It takes eleven years.

events.text: You come out of the long seclusion on a grey morning and find the gate of the grotto lit. A single paper lantern burns on the post, and beside it stands {npc}, grown, grey at the temples, who was small enough to be carried when the door shut. A pile of dead lanterns lies at {his} feet: thirty years of them, replaced each year.

choices.text: Take the lantern from {him}, and thank {him}

effects.log: You take it. It is warm in your hand. {npc} lets go slowly and says: 'It's the thirty-first.' There is a long silence, and a quieter one after it.

choices.text: Ask why {he} did not simply go on with life

mem.note: asked why I kept the lantern

effects.log: 'I did,' {npc} says. 'I also lit the lantern.' It is not a reproach, and it is the whole reproach, in four words.

choices.text: Say you were close to a breakthrough, and could not stop

effects.log: {npc} nods. It is the truth, and a fine reason, and it lands exactly like a stone. 'I understand,' {he} says, and goes in to light the stoves.

events.text: The house has changed in thirty years. A new gate. A new gardener. {npc}'s own child, a small solemn thing, sits on the stair, and looks at you with grave interest. 'Who is the old one?' the little one asks. 'My parent says the old one lives in a hole.' {npc} goes the colour of a persimmon.

choices.text: Laugh, and say it is true

effects.log: 'I do live in a hole,' you say. 'A very good one. Would you like to see?' The little one considers. {npc} laughs aloud, first in thirty years.

choices.text: Kneel and introduce yourself properly

effects.log: You kneel on the stair and give your name, with the full bow, as to an elder. The little one returns it to the inch. A thing is mended that you did not know was broken.

choices.text: Ask {npc} why the child was told that

mem.note: asked why I was a hole

effects.log: 'Because it was what I told myself,' {npc} says. 'You did not come. It was easier to say you lived in a hole.' You wince, because that is exactly as bad as it sounds.

events.text: {npc} is stiff with you for a season, and you are stiff in return. Finally, on the evening of the autumn festival, {he} sets a second lantern beside the first at the gate and says: 'The thirty-first is yours. This one is mine.' You must decide what to do with a lantern given with a condition.

choices.text: Light both together and walk out with {him}

effects.log: The two lanterns bob along the lane. Villagers on the terraces see two lights passing and say: 'Look, the two of them.' It is enough.

choices.text: Say you cannot promise not to leave again

effects.log: 'I know,' {npc} says. 'I am not asking for that. I am asking for the evening.' You give it. It is a better answer than the promise would have been.

choices.text: Leave the second lantern unlit and sit beside it

effects.log: You sit beside the unlit lantern for an hour. {npc} comes out, sits beside you, and does not light it either. The two of you watch the dark fill the lane, and call it a start.

events.text: {npc} sends a note each year after, a slip of paper with a single line, folded small, delivered by the lamp-boy at dawn. It is never a complaint. This year it reads: 'I put the lantern out. You need not do it. But if you are in a hole, there will be a light on at the gate.'

choices.text: Keep the note in your sleeve

mem.note: sent you a note a year

effects.log: You keep it in your sleeve, with the others, in a growing wad of small decencies. The seclusion door never closes quite as firmly again.

choices.text: Write back the single line: Coming.

effects.log: You write it, and fold it, and send the lamp-boy off at a trot. The answer is a small lantern, carried by hand, with a spare wick.

events.text: A new ascendant is announced at the Court gates, a mortal-born, grey, leaning on a crane's wing. The name is {npc}'s, and it is a name you have not heard spoken in four hundred years: the one who raised you in the red dust, before the Isles took you. {He} has climbed a whole lifetime of stairs to find you.

choices.text: Go to the gate yourself and take {his} arm

mem.note: came to the gate for me

effects.log: You push through the gathered clerks. {npc} sees you, and the whole climb falls from {his} face. {He} says your childhood name, which no one has used since.

choices.text: Send a servant with a barge and a welcome

effects.log: The barge is lacquered, the welcome is perfect. {npc} rides in it very straight, an honoured guest, until the servant has gone, and then slumps into the cushion.

choices.text: Stand at your own door and wait

effects.log: You wait. {npc} is led up the stair. {He} reaches your door breathless and brave, and you see in the lines of {his} face every year that you did not.

events.text: {npc} has been given a small room on the third terrace. {He} does not know which of the three tea-spoons is for guests and which for household, or how to bow to a Minister, or why the cranes are not for riding. {He} watches the Isle's immortals as one watches a play in an unknown tongue.

choices.text: Teach {him} the Isles, slowly, over tea

mem.note: taught me the Isles over tea

effects.log: Over a hundred tea-evenings, you teach {him} which spoon and which bow. {npc} learns everything except the lazy grace of someone who never expected to die, and that is, you realise, a gift.

choices.text: Find {him} a mortal-born companion among the servants

mem.note: found me someone to talk to

effects.log: The companion, an old river-woman, takes to {npc} at once. They sit all day on the third terrace, quarrelling about turnips. You are not needed, and not wounded by it.

choices.text: Take {him} down the stair to the red dust for a day

mem.note: took me home to the dust for a day

effects.log: You go together to a market in a river town. {npc} bargains with a fish-seller in dialect, a whole new person, and does not once look at the sky.

events.text: A steward of the Eight Houses calls, politely. A new ascendant of mortal birth must be assigned a House, or declared unaffiliated, within the year. {npc} has no lineage, no rank, and no wish for either. The steward has brought forms. There are seven. They are all in High Court script.

choices.text: Enrol {him} in your own House

mem.note: put me on your House roll

effects.log: You write {npc} into your own House's roll, as an honoured elder. The steward brightens: this is a form the steward knows how to file.

choices.text: Declare {him} unaffiliated, and take the stigma

effects.log: A free person above the clouds is a rare thing. The steward writes it down with the face of a man recording a scandal. {npc} signs in a plain mortal hand.

choices.text: Let {npc} read the forms and decide

effects.log: {npc} reads them one by one, slowly, with a finger under each word. {He} decides by evening, and the steward is moved to see it done with such care.

events.text: In the end it is the ordinary things. A quiet morning, a window onto the mist, {npc} dozing in a chair with a cup of cold tea in {his} hand. You sit opposite. After a lifetime above the clouds, you realise this is the first time in four hundred years that someone has had your childhood, entire, in the room with you.

choices.text: Wake {him} gently and say it aloud

mem.note: said you were glad I came

effects.log: 'I know,' {npc} says, without opening {his} eyes. 'I came for that.' You pour a second cup, and the two of you sit in the long morning.

choices.text: Let {him} sleep and keep watch

effects.log: You keep watch until noon. The cranes pass; the tea cools. When {npc} wakes, there is a blanket over {his} knees that {he} does not remember. {He} smiles, and does not ask.

events.text: {npc}, a sibling who left the old house for the Star Sea Pavilion, arrives at midnight with a lantern covered by a cloth. {He} has been speculating on futures in the Pavilion's astral exchange, and lost: nine thousand High-grade spirit stones, owed by the end of the season. {He} sits and does not meet your eyes.

choices.text: Promise to find the stones

effects.log: You promise. {npc} weeps without sound for a minute and then dries {his} face briskly, as though a cord of dignity had been retied. The stones will have to come from somewhere.

choices.text: Refuse to pay, and offer to speak with the Pavilion

mem.note: would not pay, but would speak

effects.log: {npc} nods stiffly. 'I would have refused as well,' {he} says, and does not mean it. You write to the Pavilion that night.

choices.text: Ask how it happened before saying anything else

effects.log: The story takes an hour. At the end you know: it was not greed, but a friend, a promise, and a bad night. {npc} is exhausted by the telling, and easier.

events.text: The Pavilion's debt-warden, a precise woman named Ryu Seul, arrives with a ledger the size of a door. The debt is real, Ryu Seul says, and the interest is ruinous, but the Pavilion allows alternatives to payment: a term of service, a surrender of a cultivation technique, or a pledge of the House's name.

choices.text: Offer a term of service in {npc}'s place

effects.log: You offer ten years of service. Ryu Seul writes it down with a nod. {npc} says: 'No.' You say: 'Yes.' The ledger is closed on the argument.

choices.text: Offer the House's name as a pledge

effects.log: The pledge is signed with the House seal. Ryu Seul is satisfied, and the name of the House will be asked for, in small coin, for centuries.

choices.text: Dispute the interest in front of the Pavilion's assessors

effects.log: The assessors, three tired clerks with an interest in elegance, find the compound rate non-compliant. The debt drops by a third.

events.text: Ten years on, {npc} comes to you from the Pavilion with a small box. In it lies the first fruit of a new trade {he} has built, entirely legitimate: a star-chart for river pilots, at a price pilots can afford. {He} has paid the first tenth of the debt, and sends the receipt to the Pavilion with your name.

choices.text: Take the first receipt and frame it

effects.log: The receipt hangs in the hall for a century. Guests ask about it. You say: 'My sibling's first honest day,' and are told, by the sibling, to be less charming about it.

choices.text: Return the box with a note: keep the profit

mem.note: told me to keep the profit

effects.log: You send the box back with a short note. The profit goes into the next chart-run, and the trade thrives faster.

events.text: The Pavilion's ledger is finally cleared. {npc} stands before you, and says: 'I owe you more than nine thousand.' You say the debt is closed. {He} says there is another kind of debt, and that if you refuse it, {he} will go on carrying it for the rest of {his} life, which, for an immortal, is long.

choices.text: Accept the thanks, plainly

effects.log: You accept it. It feels odd, like taking a coat. The coat fits. {npc} nods once, and the weight, at last, is somebody else's to carry.

choices.text: Say the debt of kin is not a debt at all

effects.log: {npc} frowns. 'A debt of kin is the only debt that matters,' {he} says. Then: 'Fine. I won't pay it. I'll just keep it.' It is the best you could hope for.

events.text: The Vermilion Phoenix House has called its council to name its next head, and the elders have named {npc}, who is kneeling in the middle of the vermilion hall in a borrowed robe, looking at the floor. 'I don't want the seat,' {he} says, loud enough for the back row. The council goes still as a lacquer table.

choices.text: Take {him} out of the hall and ask why

mem.note: asked me why in the corridor

effects.log: In the corridor {npc} sits on the stairs and says it plainly: the seat is a life of ledgers, and {he} wants to see the world. You listen, and the corridor is quiet for a long while.

choices.text: Tell the council {he} will accept it, in time

mem.note: told the council I would accept

effects.log: The council exhales. {npc} turns, very slowly, and the look on {his} face is not one you will forget for a century.

choices.text: Ask the council for a year to reconsider

mem.note: asked the council for a year

effects.log: The elders confer. A year is grudgingly granted. {npc} says nothing, but squeezes your hand for a moment before the council breaks.

events.text: The elder Dame Chae of the Phoenix House takes you aside, leaning on a lacquered staff. The House has no other heir of the blood who can carry the seat, Chae says. If {npc} refuses, a cousin from the Thunder Gate will be adopted in, and the Phoenix will become the Gate's feathered thing in all but name.

choices.text: Say you will not force the child, even for the House

mem.note: would not force me for the House

effects.log: Dame Chae looks at you for a long time. 'Then we will lose it,' says Dame Chae. 'Quietly.' It is the nearest thing to approval Dame Chae can give.

choices.text: Offer to hold the seat yourself until {npc} is ready

effects.log: You offer to hold the seat. Dame Chae sighs, relieved, and the House is saved for now, at a cost to the quiet of your own days.

choices.text: Ask Dame Chae whether the seat must be one person

mem.note: asked if the seat could be shared

effects.log: The old dame blinks, and then something in that old face lights. 'In nine hundred years,' says Dame Chae, 'no one has asked.' The dame goes away to read the founding charter.

events.text: The founding charter of the Phoenix House, when Dame Chae finally reads it aloud, turns out to say nothing about a single head. It speaks of 'a hearth and those who keep it'. The council debates it for a year. At the end, a council of three is proposed, with {npc} a seat among the three, chosen by {him} alone.

choices.text: Back the council of three

effects.log: The vote is close. {npc} sits at the third chair, delighted and appalled. The Phoenix has a council, and a new rule that the seat is never carried by one person's back.

choices.text: Warn that the Court may not recognise it

effects.log: The Court, when asked, is uncertain, then annoyed, then, in the end, indifferent. The council stands, a small tilt in the order of things.

events.text: {npc} walks out of the Isle at dawn with a small pack and the old cloud-compass, and does not say where. A note on the table: 'I will write when I know what I am looking for.' The House has an empty seat, a cousin from the Gate has been quietly adopted, and you have, at least, a dawn to remember.

choices.text: Stand on the dock and wave until the barge is a speck

effects.log: The barge is gone in an hour. You wave a good deal longer than that. The Phoenix has, at last, a tradition of the leaving.

choices.text: Slip a purse of spirit stones into the pack before {he} goes

mem.note: slipped a purse into my pack

effects.log: {npc} finds the purse at the first night's camp, and cries, and spends none of it for a year. When {he} does, the first thing {he} buys is a letter-brush.

events.text: Dame Noru of the Laughing River holds your newborn up to the lamp and goes quiet. Under the skin of {npc}'s palm, small as a seed, a light is turning: a spark of your own domain, God-Touched from the first breath. By custom a spark is entered in the Book of Fates within a season.

choices.text: Enter the spark in the Book of Fates, as the Court requires

mem.note: had my spark entered in the Book

effects.log: The Registrar Ilhyeon writes it down in gold, a line for the Court's records. {npc} stirs under the light, and the spark flickers in answer.

choices.text: Keep the spark within the house, and tell nobody

effects.log: You swaddle the palm in cloth and send Dame Noru away with a small gift of silence. The spark glows through the linen at night like a banked coal.

choices.text: Ask Dame Noru what such a child needs

effects.log: Dame Noru tells you in a rush: warmth, patience, an unhurried hand, and a long list of things to keep away from it. You write them all down and ignore two.

events.text: A mishap in the nursery: {npc} has a bad dream, and the spark answers. For a heartbeat the entire room is coloured by your domain, as if someone had spilled it. The lamps change hue. A nurse-god sits down hard on the floor. The infant, wholly unrepentant, gurgles.

choices.text: Calm the room with a breath of your own domain

effects.log: You draw it back like a tablecloth. The room goes back to its own colours, and the nurse-god looks at you with fresh respect and some alarm.

choices.text: Let it run and watch what the child does with it

effects.log: The room stays coloured for an hour. {npc} wakes, looks around, and laughs, and the colour fades on the laugh. You have learned something about your child, and the nurse-god about you.

choices.text: Send for Dame Noru in a hurry

mem.note: fetched Dame Noru in a panic

effects.log: Dame Noru arrives in slippers, takes in the room, and begins to laugh at you. 'Every God-Touched child does this,' says Dame Noru. 'Come and have tea.'

events.text: Registrar Ilhyeon arrives with a tutor assigned by the Court: a stern lesser god of ledgers named Gwak, who will teach {npc} the proper uses of the spark, five days in seven. {npc} regards Gwak gravely. By the second day, Gwak has been convinced to play hide-and-seek in the library.

choices.text: Let Gwak teach in the Court's way

effects.log: Gwak teaches. {npc} learns forms and limits and good manners, and the spark is trained like a vine along a wire. It grows straight, and a little cramped.

choices.text: Dismiss Gwak and teach {him} yourself

effects.log: You teach the old way, by feel and failure. The spark grows crooked and strong, and the Court sends a dry letter noting that this is not on the syllabus.

choices.text: Keep Gwak for the forms and teach the rest yourself

effects.log: A compromise. Gwak teaches the forms, you teach the feel. {npc} learns both and says, much later, that the hide-and-seek was the best lesson.

events.text: As {npc} grows, the spark takes a shape of its own: a small steady flame that follows {him} from room to room like a puppy. A cousin-god of the Long Tide, visiting, wonders aloud whether it might be taken, studied, copied. The cousin is smiling. {npc} picks up the flame protectively.

choices.text: Tell the cousin this is a child, not a specimen

mem.note: told the cousin I was not a specimen

effects.log: The cousin stops smiling. {npc} looks up at you with the flame cupped in both hands, and says: 'Thank you.' It is the first such thanks the child has given.

choices.text: Let the cousin look, but under your eye

mem.note: let the cousin study my flame

effects.log: The cousin looks, takes careful notes, and leaves an hour later, thoughtful. {npc} does not forgive the notes, but does not mind the eye.

choices.text: Make the cousin leave the house

effects.log: You see the cousin to the gate. The cousin writes you a note of grievance, and the flame, that night, curls around {npc}'s ankle like a cat.

events.text: {npc}'s spark has finally settled into its shape, and it is the exact opposite of yours: where your domain gathers, the child's scatters; where yours stills, the child's stirs. At supper a bowl of soup refuses to cool, then refuses to stay warm, then leaves the table. {npc} looks stricken.

choices.text: Laugh, and hand {him} a second bowl

mem.note: laughed with me at the soup

effects.log: The second bowl behaves for a minute and then hops to the floor, laughing, you could swear. {npc}, on the verge of tears, laughs too. The house is, after all, a house of gods.

choices.text: Explain the opposition in the Court's terms, carefully

effects.log: You explain: opposed domains are as old as the Book. They balance one another. {npc} listens and nods, and then asks if it means you will always disagree. You pause too long.

choices.text: Order the soup quietly cleared

effects.log: The bowls are carried away. {npc} watches them go and sits very still. The house feels, for a day, as if someone had quietly decided to carry the wrong thing out.

events.text: Your own domain and {npc}'s clash at the Court's Festival of the Seasons. In front of the whole assembly, a procession of the gods of harvest and rain, the child's scattering spark disturbs your gathering, and a ceremonial banner goes wildly askew. A few elder gods snigger. {npc} wants the floor to swallow {him}.

choices.text: Take the blame for the disorder yourself

effects.log: You step forward and bow to the assembly, saying it was your doing. The elders blink. {npc} stares at you with wide eyes. It is a lie, and a gentle one, and the child will never forget it.

choices.text: Let {npc} stand and explain

effects.log: {npc} stands, trembling, and says in a small clear voice that it was an accident, and that {he} is sorry. The assembly softens. A few of the elders look away, ashamed of their sniggers.

choices.text: Join your domain to {his}, and fix the banner

mem.note: joined with me at the Festival

effects.log: You and {npc} stand shoulder to shoulder and let the two sparks mix. The banner straightens itself, and the assembly claps, mildly, as at a trick.

events.text: {npc} has grown into the quarrel. {He} can scatter what you gather with a breath, and has begun to do it on purpose: little things, a shelf of scrolls knocked from its place, the household cat unravelled to its yarn and rewound. One evening {he} does it to you, at table, with a bright, defiant eye.

choices.text: Let it pass, and rewind your own thread

effects.log: You rewind your thread with a sigh. {npc} watches you with a shade of disappointment, as if hoping for a fight and denied one.

choices.text: Stand against {his} scattering with your whole domain

ok.log: You hold. {npc}'s scatter breaks like surf on a stone. {He} stares, then grins, shaky and delighted, and says: 'I was hoping.'

fail.log: The scatter goes through you like wind through paper. You gather yourself. {npc} is stricken at what {he} did, and apologises for a week.

choices.text: Ask {him} to teach you what the scatter feels like

mem.note: asked what the scatter felt like

effects.log: {npc} blinks. Nobody has asked. {He} sits across from you and describes, haltingly, what it is to be a thing that loosens. By dawn you have learned a thing you did not know.

events.text: The two sparks, yours and {npc}'s, are called to a joint rite at the Court: the Rite of the Balance, in which opposed domains of one family stand in the chambers of the Book and are weighed. It is a rare honour, and a risk. The Book is said to find in each pair either a union or a rift.

choices.text: Stand in the Balance together

mem.note: stood in the Balance with me

effects.log: You stand with {npc}. The Book weighs you, and what it finds is written in a column of light. The word is Balance, not Rift. {npc} cries, and cannot say why.

choices.text: Decline the rite and keep the quarrel private

effects.log: You decline. The Court is surprised, then a little disappointed. {npc} is relieved and never says so, and the quarrel remains the household's own.

events.text: The soup, which has been escaping the table for years, finally stays. One evening {npc} sets a bowl in front of you, and it steams and does not move, and you both look at it. 'I did that,' {npc} says, wondering. 'On purpose.' You taste it. It is neither hot nor cold, and entirely perfect.

choices.text: Say it is the best soup you have ever had

effects.log: {npc} laughs, and the laugh is a scatter of silver light across the table, and your domain gathers it into a cup. The two of you drink it together.

choices.text: Ask how {he} held it still

mem.note: told you how I held the soup

effects.log: {npc} explains: not by gathering, which is yours, but by listening, which is {his}. You write this down in your head, as a note on how the opposite of a thing is not its enemy.

events.text: A village in a mortal world far below has noticed that its fields have been green since the week {npc} was born, and has put two and two together with the village priest, Brother Mal. A shrine has been raised: a clay doll of the infant in a niche, with a bowl of millet and a prayer to a child who cannot yet walk.
events.arc: A Child Prayed To Before Walking

choices.text: Accept the worship, and send a blessing

effects.log: A soft rain falls on the village, exactly sufficient. The village is delirious with joy. {npc}, in the cradle, claps for the sound of it without knowing why.

choices.text: Send word to Brother Mal that the child is not a god yet
