effects.log: Brother Mal receives the word in tears and is stricken with remorse. The shrine is renamed 'the House of the Little One's Hearth', and the prayers are less direct and more tender.

choices.text: Do nothing, and watch the faith gather

effects.log: The faith gathers in a bowl in the Court's receiving hall, small, warm, and a little puzzled. {npc} sleeps beside it. You are not sure what you have set going.

events.text: The village's prayers keep coming up through the floor of heaven, and they are very specific. A boy's cough. A well gone dry. A bride's fever. They are addressed to {npc}, who is nine months old and unable to answer so much as a rattle. The prayers pile up like laundry.
events.arc: A Child Prayed To Before Walking

choices.text: Answer them yourself in the child's name

mem.note: answered my prayers in my name

effects.log: You answer the prayers in {npc}'s name, small ones first. The village thanks the child. The child, learning to crawl, receives the thanks in the form of a moulded clay doll sent upwards.

choices.text: Let the prayers lie, and send a single clear sign

effects.log: You send a single sign, a cloud shaped like a sleeping child. The prayers thin to a trickle, as the village decides this means 'wait'.

choices.text: Pass the prayers on to a minor hearth-god of your acquaintance

mem.note: passed on my prayers to a hearth-god

effects.log: A small hearth-god, grateful for the work, takes the prayers on. The village notices only that the cough clears, and they are, at last, grateful to the right quarter.

events.text: The Court takes notice. Registrar Ilhyeon calls on you with an ominous scroll: a child under ten years may not hold a shrine, as a matter of the Book. The faith gathered at {npc}'s doll must be redirected, or the child will be struck for a premature elevation.
events.arc: A Child Prayed To Before Walking

choices.text: Redirect the faith to a shared altar of the family

mem.note: moved my shrine to the family altar

effects.log: The faith is poured into your own altar, and the clay doll is moved to a niche beside it, a small mortal sibling to a god. Ilhyeon signs, grudgingly.

choices.text: Argue that the village built the shrine unprompted

mem.note: argued my shrine before the Court

effects.log: A long argument, with cited precedents. Ilhyeon is not persuaded, but the precedent is, and the case is entered in the Book as a question to be examined in a century.

choices.text: Close the shrine yourself, quietly

effects.log: You close it with a long letter to Brother Mal. The shrine becomes a plain chapel to the hearth. {npc} never learns what was lost, and you carry it alone.

events.text: A pilgrim from the village, an old woman with a staff and a satchel of millet-cakes, arrives at the edge of the Court after a lifetime's walk, and asks to see the child the village has prayed to for twelve years. {npc}, who is now a long-limbed, ink-stained twelve, stares from the doorway at the old woman's eyes.
events.arc: A Child Prayed To Before Walking

choices.text: Let {npc} receive the pilgrim, and stand behind {him}

mem.note: met my pilgrim with you behind me

effects.log: {npc} takes the satchel, bows, and begins to speak. The old woman weeps. It is a shy, correct, awkward encounter, and the best-natured miracle of the age.

choices.text: Receive the pilgrim yourself and carry the thanks to the child

effects.log: The pilgrim kneels to you and calls you the child's keeper. The pilgrim is wrong, and a little right, and goes home content.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what {he} would like to say to the pilgrim

mem.note: asked me what I wanted to say

effects.log: {npc} thinks, seriously. 'Thank you,' {he} says. 'And please stop making me a doll.' The pilgrim, hearing it relayed, laughs for a quarter hour.

events.text: Among the prayers that reach you, one comes in a voice you know: {npc}, born of a mortal mother in a river world, praying for a good harvest at a shrine {he} thinks belongs to a distant, uncaring god. {He} does not know. The prayer is clumsy, sweet, and addressed, as it happens, to you.
events.arc: The Prayer of a Mortal-Born Child

choices.text: Answer in silence, with a good harvest

mem.note: got my harvest and did not know

effects.log: The harvest comes in heavy and fat. {npc} gives thanks to the shrine, and the shrine, for the first time in your hearing, is full of love for the right god.

choices.text: Listen, and say nothing at all

effects.log: You listen to the prayer to the end, and it is simply a prayer. You do not move a leaf. {npc} finishes, and goes to bed, and the harvest, unanswered, is simply weather.

choices.text: Send a dream with your voice in it

effects.log: That night {npc} dreams of a high place and a voice that knows {his} name, saying only: 'Well done.' {He} wakes weeping, and cannot say why.

events.text: The years go by below, as years do. {npc} prays more often, always the same shrine, always to the same imagined god. The prayers have changed: they are no longer for a harvest but for ordinary company, a friend, a word. You hear every one. A mortal's loneliness is a heavy prayer to hold.
events.arc: The Prayer of a Mortal-Born Child

choices.text: Send a friend into {his} life, a travelling pedlar

effects.log: A pedlar with a limp turns up at {npc}'s door in the rain, seeking shelter, and stays three days. The pedlar becomes a visitor, then a friend, then a name in the prayers.

choices.text: Let the loneliness be what it is

effects.log: You let it be. A mortal's heart can carry what it carries. But you hear each prayer, and each time you cannot answer, something in you goes a little more silent.

choices.text: Descend as a stranger, for a single day

mem.note: served you rice and did not know

effects.log: You walk into the river-village in plain clothes and ask for a bowl of rice. {npc} serves you. You talk about the weather, and the price of reeds, and for one day you are, simply, a customer.

events.text: {npc} comes to the shrine one grey dusk and says the old prayer, then adds a new line: 'I think I know who you are. If you are the one I think, there is no need to answer. I only wanted to say it aloud.' The shrine is cold. {He} bows. The reed-wind passes through the doorway.
events.arc: The Prayer of a Mortal-Born Child

choices.text: Answer: a single warm breath on {his} neck

effects.log: A breath of warm air touches {npc}'s neck, the way a parent's would. {He} stays very still. 'I knew,' {he} whispers. 'Thank you.' The shrine does not feel cold afterwards.

choices.text: Stay silent, and let {him} keep the not-knowing

effects.log: You stay silent. {npc} bows again and goes home, and the line of the prayer settles into the shrine like an offering. Some things are better held than confirmed.

choices.text: Appear to {him} in the shrine, in full light

effects.log: You appear. The shrine is bathed in gold. {npc} falls to {his} knees, and then, shakily, stands. 'You came,' {he} says. It is the best and worst thing you could have done.

events.text: Mortal years run short. {npc} has grown grey, and a cough has come that no herb cures. {He} prays at the shrine one more dusk, and the prayer is brief: 'I have been well. Thank you.' It is carried up through the Court on the wings of a thousand others, and reaches you at the end of a long day.
events.arc: The Prayer of a Mortal-Born Child

choices.text: Go down to the bedside at the end

effects.log: You go. The room is plain, the lamp small. {npc} sees you and does not look away. The last words are plain ones. Afterward, the shrine is full of the smell of millet.

choices.text: Hold the prayer, and answer it with a harvest of the whole valley

effects.log: The valley's harvest is the best in a hundred years. The whole village thanks the shrine at the funeral. {npc} would have been mortified.

events.text: The prayer stops one season, between one dusk and the next. The shrine is empty. A last offering of millet sits dry in its bowl, left by a neighbour. There is, you find, a place in the Court's hall where the prayers of a thousand lie, and in it one that does not rise any more.
events.arc: The Prayer of a Mortal-Born Child

choices.text: Take the last millet to the Court's altar and offer it

effects.log: You carry the bowl up the stair and offer it to the lamp, in {npc}'s name. The Court's hall dims for a moment, as if bowing.

choices.text: Leave the shrine standing, with a new light

mem.note: left a light at my shrine

effects.log: You send a little hearth-flame to burn there, as long as there are reeds in the river. The village will say it is a miracle. They will be right.

events.text: Registrar Ilhyeon opens the Book of Fates to {npc}'s page and cannot find a domain to write. The spark in the child is real, bright and unlike anything on any list of the twelve. It does not match a god of the Court. It does not match the dead. 'It has no name,' the Registrar says, honestly.

choices.text: Ask the Registrar to write a new page

effects.log: Ilhyeon blanches. A new page is a matter for the council, Ilhyeon says, and takes months. The paperwork is started at once, which is a promise a god of that kind can keep.

choices.text: Tell {npc} the spark needs no name

mem.note: said my spark needs no name

effects.log: {npc} listens with a face of such open relief that you realise {he} was dreading the label. {He} says: 'Then I can just be me.' And then, after a moment: 'Is that allowed?'

choices.text: Search the old lore for an extinct domain

mem.note: searched the lore for my domain

effects.log: You spend a season in the Unlit Lamp's archive. The answer is not an extinct domain but a missing one, the faint outline of a thing that once existed between two others. You are not certain what you have found.

events.text: The spark does strange things. It leaves no mark on anything {npc} does for it, but the houses around them become, somehow, more themselves: a baker's bread rises better, a poet's verse finds a rhyme, a worried husband remembers the forgotten thing. The Court begins to take an interest.

choices.text: Keep a ledger of what the spark does

mem.note: kept a ledger of my spark

effects.log: You keep a ledger. After a year it has four hundred entries and a pattern. The pattern is not a domain. It is a sort of kindness that the other domains forgot to be.

choices.text: Ask the neighbours what they feel

effects.log: The neighbours have nothing definite. 'It is,' says one, 'like being remembered.' A god of the Hidden Star, overhearing, goes pale, and walks away fast.

choices.text: Keep the Court away from the house

mem.note: kept the Court from my door

effects.log: You send the Court's inquirers away with a polite refusal. They come back with a better letter. The matter is not closed, only postponed.

events.text: The council of the Court meets in the Hall of the Twelve to decide whether {npc}'s spark may have a page. The elder gods are divided. Elder Baram of the Nine Wells argues for it. A lord of the Hidden Star argues against. {npc} sits in the corner of the vast hall, hands in {his} lap, trying to look unremarkable.

choices.text: Speak for {npc} before the council

mem.note: spoke for me before the Twelve

effects.log: You speak, briefly, of a child, and a bakery, and a rhyme. A hush. Elder Baram rises to second you. The vote is not unanimous, but it is enough.

choices.text: Let {npc} speak for {him}

mem.note: spoke for myself before the Twelve

effects.log: {npc} stands and says one sentence, and sits. The sentence is: 'I do not mind if there is no page.' The hall is silent. The page is written in a hush.

choices.text: Withdraw the petition and spare {him} the hall

effects.log: You rise and withdraw it. The Hidden Star lord looks smug. {npc} looks at you, unsure whether to be grateful or hurt, and chooses the first.

events.text: {npc} grows up a god without a domain, which is to say, a god of whatever is needed. The village below prays to {him} without a name, a hundred prayers a year, in the blank spaces of other prayers. {He} answers them in the small hours, in the corners of the world no domain reaches.

choices.text: Keep {him} company in the small hours

mem.note: sat with me through the blank prayers

effects.log: You sit beside {npc} through the night as the blank prayers arrive. There is more room in the world than the twelve account for. {He} is the proof, and you the first to sit with the proof.

choices.text: Leave {him} to it and trust {him}

mem.note: was trusted with the blank prayers

effects.log: You leave. {npc} manages. In the morning there is a hand-drawn star-map on your desk: a gift, with no label, drawn in the margins of what is not on any map.

events.text: A wind-borne letter falls from the sleeve of {npc}, a sibling god of your Lineage, as {he} bows out of a council. It is in your House's own old cipher, addressed to Cheongsa, the envoy of another pantheon, and it offers the seating of the Lineage's harvest-rolls for the coming age. {He} has not noticed it fall.

choices.text: Confront {him} in the empty corridor

effects.log: You hold out the letter. {npc} looks at it, then at you, and for a moment all the faces of a sibling pass across {his} face. 'I was going to tell you,' {he} says. It is a lie, and a decent one.

choices.text: Put the letter back in the sleeve and watch

mem.note: let me carry the letter on

effects.log: You return it with a light hand. For a season you watch every move {npc} makes. It is a cold, lonely season, and you learn more of your sibling than you did in an age.

choices.text: Burn the letter at the nearest lamp

effects.log: The cipher goes up in a bright flash. No one will ever know what it said, except you, and you will know it for ages. {npc} never learns of the near-miss and bows to you the next day with a serene face.

events.text: Cheongsa's envoy-barge docks at the Court, hung with banners of another pantheon, and {npc} is waiting at the stair, dressed for a feast. The two of you are seated side by side at the opening banquet. {He} pours your tea with a steady hand, and talks lightly of old gods, as if nothing at all were in {his} sleeve.

choices.text: Watch the envoy and {npc} through the whole banquet

mem.note: sat by me at the banquet

effects.log: You see the envoy's glance at {npc} three times, and {npc}'s glance back, once. The glances are brief and exact, and add up to a conspiracy in the margins of a feast.

choices.text: Raise a toast to the Lineage's unbroken faith

effects.log: The toast rings. {npc}'s cup trembles by a hair. The envoy drinks smoothly. You are, between them, a thin line, and know it.

choices.text: Leave the banquet early, and take {npc} with you

effects.log: You murmur an excuse and steer {him} out by the elbow. In the corridor {he} says, 'Why?' You say you wanted to talk. 'About what?' You find, to your surprise, that you do not know.

events.text: The Heavenly Court convenes the Hall of Vows. The Lineage's harvest-rolls have been seen in another pantheon's hands, and the Court seeks the leak. {npc} stands before the Twelve in the white of the accused, and looks across the hall to you. You hold the evidence of the letter in your memory, in full.

choices.text: Testify truthfully, and take the consequences

ok.log: You speak. The Hall listens. The Twelve find against {npc}, but mildly: a century's exile to a quiet world, not an unmaking. {He} bows to you as the sentence is read. It is not a thank you.

fail.log: You speak, and the Hall is unconvinced: the evidence is missing a clause. {npc} is acquitted by a hair, and looks at you with a perfect, flat gratitude.

choices.text: Speak for the defence, and keep the letter to yourself

mem.note: spoke for me at the Hall

effects.log: You speak for {npc}'s long service. The Twelve are moved, and the case is dismissed for want of proof. {npc} says nothing at all, and the quiet is a debt that grows.

events.text: A blight falls on a world your Lineage keeps: the harvest-rolls, which {npc} gave away without anyone's knowing, have been misapplied by another pantheon's hands, and the wheat is rotting in the ear. A thousand prayers rise, specific and unanswerable. {npc} comes to you in the night, grey, and tells you everything.

choices.text: Forgive {him}, and mend the blight together

effects.log: You and {npc} work the whole night with the harvest-rolls, correcting each misapplication by hand. At dawn the wheat is standing again. Neither of you says a word about the forgiving.

choices.text: Send {him} to the Court to confess alone

effects.log: {npc} goes. The Court is merciful, and the sentence is light. But {he} goes alone, and does not look back at you in the doorway.

choices.text: Mend the blight and keep {his} guilt secret

effects.log: You mend it alone, quickly, with only the minor gods of the harvest to see. {npc} is spared the Court and never quite forgives you for that, in the way of the saved.

events.text: Elder Gahee of {npc}'s Lineage arrives at your temple in the black of a formal visit, with three scribes and a scroll. The Lineage wishes, Gahee says, to see your domain settled upon the union as a dowry, and the Divine Consort's seat in your halls made the Lineage's. It is phrased as an honour.

choices.text: Refuse the claim, in front of the scribes

mem.note: refused my Lineage in front of me

effects.log: You refuse. Elder Gahee's pen does not even pause. 'We expected as much,' says Gahee. 'Consider it the first of three.' {npc} stands very still.

choices.text: Offer a share of the domain, not the whole of it

effects.log: Elder Gahee tilts that stern head. 'A share is a beginning,' says Gahee. The scribes write industriously. {npc} watches your face as if reading a book in a language {he} is just learning.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what {he} wants before answering anyone

effects.log: The room freezes. Elder Gahee stares at {npc}. {npc} stares at you. 'No one has ever asked me,' {he} says, very low. The scribes put down their pens.

events.text: The next week, a pair of the Lineage's lesser gods turn up as guests of the household, charmingly. They admire your temple. They compliment the cook. They measure the walls, in passing, with a ribbon. {npc} watches them from a window with a shut face, hands behind {his} back.

choices.text: Ask the guests plainly why they are measuring

mem.note: asked the guests what they measured

effects.log: They tell you, blandly: it is a courtesy, to prepare a seat. {npc} does not smile. Neither do you. Within the hour they have politely gone.

choices.text: Invite the guests to dine and learn the Lineage's mind

effects.log: Over a dinner of eleven courses, the guests let slip that the Lineage's faith is thin and it wants yours. {npc} listens and says nothing, but afterwards, at the window, leans against your shoulder.

choices.text: Have the guests quietly shown out

effects.log: The guests are shown out by a servant. By evening the Lineage has sent a stiff note. By midnight the whole Court knows. {npc} says: 'That was one way to do it.'

events.text: Elder Gahee returns, and this time brings an old, kind face as well: {npc}'s eldest aunt-in-spirit, who smells of dried apricot and raised {him} through the dark ages. The aunt does not demand. The aunt asks, with hands in the lap of an apricot-scented robe: 'Is it so terrible to belong to a thing larger than yourself?'

choices.text: Answer honestly: it depends who owns the thing

effects.log: The aunt blinks. Elder Gahee frowns. {npc} looks at you with an expression of astonished love. The aunt, unexpectedly, laughs: 'Quite right.' The scroll is left on the table.

choices.text: Say the Lineage may keep a seat, but not the domain

effects.log: The aunt nods slowly. 'A seat,' says the aunt. 'That I can carry back.' Elder Gahee is not pleased, but is outranked by an apricot-scented relative.

choices.text: Say yes to the aunt, for love of {npc}

mem.note: gave away your domain for me

effects.log: You say yes. The scroll is signed on the spot. {npc} goes white, then red, then very still. 'I did not ask you to,' {he} says. 'I know,' you say. It is the wrong answer, and the true one.

events.text: The part of your domain that you ceded to the Lineage begins to behave oddly. It answers to the wrong prayers. Rains arrive in the wrong valleys. A small god of the shallows, who used to answer to you, is now answering to Elder Gahee's cousins, and brings you a note of apology, in tears.

choices.text: Reclaim the share by a ritual of the Book

mem.note: stayed at my side for the rite

effects.log: The rite takes a month and an old debt. When it is done the share is yours again, and the Lineage is seething. {npc} stays at your side the whole month and says nothing.

choices.text: Let the Lineage keep it and learn what it costs them

mem.note: let my Lineage learn the cost

effects.log: You wait. The Lineage's cousins misapply the share, and by the second season the Elder returns, contrite and very polite, to ask whether you would take it back. {npc} laughs aloud, first in a year.

events.text: Elder Gahee's letter arrives on the thinnest paper in the Court. It is very short. It says that the Lineage has reviewed its claim, and withdrawn it; that the seat will remain a seat; that {npc} is to be reminded that a Lineage's favour is a thing given, not a debt owed. It is signed, at the bottom, with a small drawing of an apricot.

choices.text: Frame the apricot and hang it in the hall

effects.log: The apricot is framed in gold wire. {npc} laughs until {he} has to sit down, and the Lineage, hearing of it, sends a basket of the real fruit.

choices.text: Write back a modest, grateful reply

effects.log: Your reply is three lines and the drawing of a small cloud. The Lineage replies with an apricot. A tradition is born, and lasts several ages.

events.text: A thin notice arrives from the Heavenly Court under Registrar Ilhyeon's seal: {npc}'s page in the Book of Fates has been struck. No reason given beyond a clause about 'irregular elevation'. A god with no page is a god not counted: no prayers, no temple, no thread, no place at any table.
events.arc: A Name Struck from the Book

choices.text: Appeal to the Twelve at once

effects.log: You file the appeal that evening, on the thickest parchment. Ilhyeon accepts it with a pained look. Appeals of this kind take a century, Ilhyeon says, and the page is struck for the duration.

choices.text: Take {npc} to a mortal world and live there unwritten

effects.log: You pack a small bag and slip out of the Court in the dusk. {npc}, silent, holds your hand. Below, in the dust, nothing is written, and nothing can be struck.

choices.text: Forge a new page in the Book yourself

effects.log: You steal into the lower vault with a borrowed pen. The forgery is perfect and is the worst thing you have ever done. {npc} learns of it, and is horrified, and grateful, and does not know where to put either.

events.text: Without a page, {npc} grows faint. The household's lamps no longer light at {his} approach. The temple doors do not open. Unmyeong, god of fate, passes {him} in the corridor and flinches: the thread that used to tie {npc} to the Weaver's loom hangs loose and dull, with a frayed end.
events.arc: A Name Struck from the Book

choices.text: Tie the loose thread to yourself

effects.log: You knot it to your own wrist. It holds, and {npc} regains a thin colour, though a god bound to another is half a god, and you feel the weight of it every day.

choices.text: Ask Unmyeong for a thread of honest making

effects.log: Unmyeong, after a long look, hands you a new thread with the air of a clerk breaking a rule. It is thin and plain. {npc} wears it as a bracelet and does not speak of it.

choices.text: Say nothing and keep {npc} close

mem.note: kept me close when I was uncounted

effects.log: You keep {him} close, and nothing moves. The days are quiet. {npc} learns to be present without being counted, which is a rare and uncomfortable art.

events.text: The Heavenly Court's hearing is called, at last. Twelve elders, a gallery of scribes, and a single stool at the centre of the hall. The Registrar reads the charge: 'irregular elevation'. It turns out that {npc}'s page was struck because a rival Lineage, years ago, registered a complaint, and no one thought to withdraw it.
events.arc: A Name Struck from the Book

choices.text: Argue the complaint was malicious

effects.log: You argue, with documents. The elders confer. The complaint is found to have been filed by a god of the Hidden Star who is no longer in the Court. The strike is lifted, with an apology that is almost sincere.

choices.text: Let {npc} speak to the elders

effects.log: {npc}, small on the stool, speaks for four sentences. The elders are quiet. At the end, Elder Baram says: 'The Book does not strike what it has not understood.' The page is restored in the same breath.

choices.text: Demand the complaint be struck instead

ok.log: You demand, and the hall hears the weight of a god who has stood in the Court for ages. The complaint is struck, and {npc}'s page returns. It is a victory, though a loud one.

fail.log: You demand, and the hall demurs. The elders do not like being demanded of. The appeal is set back another ten years, and {npc} sits on the stool, patiently, through the whole of it.

events.text: In the dust of a small mortal world, {npc} has learned to live without a page. {He} bakes bread with a neighbour's family, and nobody asks what god {he} is. Occasionally a prayer rises, from a village woman, unsure of its address, and {npc} stops kneading and listens to it, and answers it, unwritten.
events.arc: A Name Struck from the Book

choices.text: Stay below with {him}, as a neighbour

effects.log: You stay. The years go by in bread and rain, and the Court forgets, and the sky forgets. There is a peace in being unwritten that is hard to describe to the written.

choices.text: Go back to the Court and ask for the page, on {his} behalf

effects.log: You go back and ask. The Court is hesitant. Finally, grudgingly, the page is restored with a footnote: 'by request of a parent'. {npc} refuses to read the footnote and is delighted by it.

events.text: A prayer from the lower worlds arrives in a bewildered hand: the hail came in the month of blossom, the rivers ran backwards, and the harvest burned in the field. The weather and the harvest of four valleys are in the keeping of your Lineage, and the cause is a quarrel at your own long table between {npc}, an elder of the Lineage, and your sibling.
events.arc: The Family That Hailed on Itself

choices.text: Go to the table and make the family sit

effects.log: You seat them, one at each end, and go to fetch the tea. The sky over four valleys holds its breath. {npc}, reaching for the pot, finds your hand already on it.

choices.text: Take {npc}'s side openly, as an elder

mem.note: sided with me against your sibling

effects.log: You side with {npc}. The hail, which had been wild, becomes aimed. The farmers below begin to pray for a new god of weather, and a rumour starts of a new Lineage.

choices.text: Mend the harvest below and leave the quarrel to burn out

effects.log: You mend the harvest in secret, one valley at a time. The quarrel grows more fierce in your absence. The farmers are fed. The family is not.

events.text: The weather over the valleys is a map of the family. Hail where {npc} sits angriest, drought where your sibling sulks, an unseasonal warmth over the one valley where a cousin has quietly begun to smile. A village headwoman prays: please, whoever you are, tell the family to go to bed.
events.arc: The Family That Hailed on Itself

choices.text: Send the headwoman a sign of a cloud shaped like a closed door

mem.note: sent a cloud as a door

effects.log: The headwoman understands, to your surprise, and takes the village indoors for three days. The weather rampages past the shut doors and passes.

choices.text: Answer the prayer in your own voice, from the sky

effects.log: You say, in a voice that carries: 'We are sorry. Go to bed.' The village sleeps. The family, overhearing, goes slightly pink.

choices.text: Use the headwoman's prayer to shame the family at the table

effects.log: You read the prayer aloud at supper. The table is stunned. {npc} leaves the table, pale. The sky over the valleys, for the first time in a season, turns grey and does nothing.

events.text: The family sits to supper at last, and no one speaks until the soup is cold. At length {npc} puts down a spoon and says that the quarrel began, you will recall, over a borrowed cloud-barge, four hundred years ago, and has gained interest. 'I should like to apologise,' {he} says, 'but I have forgotten whose fault it was.'
events.arc: The Family That Hailed on Itself

choices.text: Say it was nobody's, and pass the rice

mem.note: passed the rice and ended it

effects.log: You pass the rice. Slowly, over the course of an hour, the supper warms. By the end the sibling and {npc} are arguing, happily, about the proper way to boil an egg.

choices.text: Say it was the sibling's, and mean it

effects.log: The sibling stiffens. The hail starts again, a light scatter. You have given the family a verdict and lost the supper, and it will take a century to see which mattered.

choices.text: Say it was yours, as the one who lent the barge

effects.log: A pause. Then: 'You lent the barge?' {npc} says. 'Of course you did.' The laughter that follows is a complete surprise, and it takes the quarrel out of the room like a draught.

events.text: The weather over the valleys becomes a campaign. {npc}'s hail is answered by your sibling's drought, which is answered by a flood from a cousin who never wanted any part. The farmers below have started building their granaries on stilts. The Heavenly Court, at length, sends a quiet letter: end it, or be ended.
events.arc: The Family That Hailed on Itself

choices.text: Go before the Court and take a share of the blame

mem.note: took a share of the blame

effects.log: You stand in the Hall of the Twelve and say that the family has been at fault, and you with it. The Court, startled by the honesty, reduces the penalty to a fine in faith.

choices.text: Call a family council at the harvest altar

mem.note: called the council at the altar

effects.log: You call it. They come, one by one, to the altar of the old harvest, and kneel for the first time in an age to the same stone. The hail stops at the altar's edge.

events.text: {npc}, the old god who bore your Lineage out of a dying domain, comes to your hall by foot, which a god of that age never does. The light around {him} is thin, like a lamp at the end of its oil. The last of {his} temples closed this spring. {He} says: 'I wished to see the house once more, while I am still visible.'

choices.text: Lend {him} a share of your own faith

effects.log: You open a channel of the prayers that rise to you and let a thread of them flow to {npc}. The light thickens by a shade. {He} says, 'You did not have to,' and lets it run.

choices.text: Invite {him} to stay in your temple, as a guest

mem.note: gave me a room in your temple

effects.log: You offer a guest-room in your temple. Pilgrims, passing, bow to the old god without knowing why. Some of that bowing is enough to keep a flame lit.

choices.text: Honour {him} with a farewell, and do not interfere

effects.log: You hold a farewell feast in the old style, with a hundred minor gods and an empty chair. {npc} eats lightly, and smiles, and leaves at dawn without looking back.

events.text: The old god and the young gods of the household get along better than either expected. {npc} tells stories in the evenings of the First Hour, when there were no domains yet, only weather and appetite. The younger gods sit on the floor and listen, and ask foolish questions, and are answered with great patience.

choices.text: Write down the stories as {he} tells them

effects.log: You fill nine scrolls with the stories of the First Hour. The Unlit Lamp's librarians, hearing, send three scribes to copy them, and {npc} becomes, for the first time in an age, a source.

choices.text: Sit among the young gods and ask the foolish questions yourself

mem.note: let me ask the foolish questions

effects.log: You ask whether there was always a sun. {npc} laughs, a sound like a long-unused bell. 'No,' {he} says. 'There was only a very large wish.' You do not write that down. You keep it.

choices.text: Fetch a poet to set the stories in verse

mem.note: brought a poet for my stories

effects.log: A poet of the Laughing River comes, and for a season the household is full of rhymes. {npc} is bashful and flattered, and corrects the metre.

events.text: {npc} grows more solid with each season: the lent faith, the stories, the pilgrims bowing. One morning {he} stands in the hall in full light, as {he} has not in ten thousand years, and says: 'I have a temple again. A very small one. In the corner of your garden. Would you mind?' You find the stone laid in the night.

choices.text: Build the shrine in marble

effects.log: You build it in marble, with a roof of grey cloud-slate. {npc} touches the lintel, and the shrine accepts the touch. The first pilgrim comes within the month.

choices.text: Leave the stone as it is, and let the garden take it

effects.log: The stone remains unfinished, and the moss grows over it, and the old god's first visitors arrive through the hedge. The shrine is, in its own way, a perfect thing.

events.text: {npc} is gone before you know it. The guest-room is empty, the bed unslept in, a single white feather on the pillow. A note, in the thinnest ink: 'I did not want to be seen to go. Thank you for the house.' The note is not signed. It does not need to be.

choices.text: Keep the room as it is, with the feather

mem.note: kept my room as it was

effects.log: You keep it, door ajar, and the feather on the pillow. Visitors ask. You say: 'Someone old, and dear.' The room never gathers dust.

choices.text: Send out every minor god of the household to look

effects.log: They search three worlds in a day. They find, at last, only a very small fire in the hearth of a village, and a smell of old incense. It is enough. It is a kind of answer.

events.text: The Lineage of the Silent Drum, which respects only those who fought in heaven, has chosen a consort-god for {npc}: Lord Cheon, a general of a vanished war, scarred, grave, and four thousand years older. It is a great honour. It is announced before the household. {npc} lifts {his} chin and looks at the wall.

choices.text: Ask {npc} in private whether {he} wishes it

effects.log: The door is closed. {npc} sits down. 'No,' {he} says. 'But I don't wish to shame you.' You say that shame is yours to carry, not {his}, and the silence that follows is longer than the war.

choices.text: Accept the honour on the Lineage's terms

effects.log: You accept, with a bow. {npc} stands by your side and does not move a muscle. Lord Cheon inclines that scarred head, and the household breathes.

choices.text: Ask the Silent Drum for a year before answering

mem.note: asked the Drum for a year

effects.log: The Lineage grants it, as a courtesy that does not quite hide its pique. {npc} says: 'Thank you.' The year begins.

events.text: Lord Cheon calls at the household, scarred and silent, with a gift: a small war-drum, no bigger than a bowl. Lord Cheon sets it on the table and says it has not been struck in four thousand years, and does not offer to strike it. {npc} regards the drum, then the general, and is at last, tentatively, curious.

choices.text: Leave them alone with the drum

mem.note: left me alone with Lord Cheon

effects.log: You leave. An hour later, from the hall, comes the sound of a single stroke on a very small drum, and then a long conversation.

choices.text: Stay, and ask Lord Cheon about the war

mem.note: asked Lord Cheon about the war

effects.log: Lord Cheon tells the war in six sentences, and the hall goes cold. {npc} listens to the end. Afterward Lord Cheon says to you: 'I did not know anyone would ask.'

choices.text: Warn Lord Cheon that {npc} has not agreed

mem.note: warned the general I had not agreed

effects.log: The general bows. 'Neither have I,' says Lord Cheon. 'I was ordered.' A small shock for you both. The two of you sit down, and a different conversation begins.

events.text: The decision comes at last, on the last day of the year. {npc} comes to your study in formal robes, with Lord Cheon at {his} side, and says that after some months of difficult conversation, the two of them have reached an arrangement. It is not the arrangement that was announced. It is, however, entirely theirs.

choices.text: Listen to the arrangement, and bless it

effects.log: It is a partnership of a sort the Book has no word for: friendship, a shared study of an old war, and a seat for each at the other's hearth. You bless it in the old words.

choices.text: Tell them the Lineage will never accept it

effects.log: Lord Cheon smiles for the first time in your hearing. 'The Lineage,' says Lord Cheon, 'can speak with me.' {npc} squeezes that scarred hand. You see, rather late, that you were never the obstacle.

events.text: {npc} is wed to Lord Cheon at the next equinox, without joy and without protest, in the Hall of the Silent Drum. The drum is struck three times. {He} stands at the end of the long hall in a robe of black and bronze, and when it is over, comes down the steps toward you, and does not meet your eye.

choices.text: Meet {his} eye anyway, and open your arms

mem.note: opened your arms at the wedding

effects.log: {npc} stops, a pace away. 'I did not forgive you,' {he} says. 'Not yet.' You say you know. {He} steps in, stiffly, and for a moment is again very small.

choices.text: Congratulate the new Divine Consort formally

mem.note: bowed to me at the wedding

effects.log: You bow, correctly. {npc} bows back, correctly, with a flicker of something like grief. It is the last time the two of you are formal for a very long time.

events.text: A young god arrives at your hall with a travelling-case and a sullen look: {npc}, your Divine Consort's child from an earlier union, sent by a Lineage to live in your house for the Court season. {He} stands in the doorway and says, to nobody in particular, that this is clearly the wrong address.

choices.text: Welcome {him} as a guest of rank

effects.log: You offer the guest-suite, a seat at table and a tour. {npc} answers in monosyllables, and the household does what it can with the silence.

choices.text: Welcome {him} as one of the house

effects.log: You show {npc} to a room with a view of the garden and say that it is {his} for as long as {he} wishes. {He} stares at the key as though it were a small snake.

choices.text: Ask your Consort how to approach {him}

mem.note: asked my parent how to approach me

effects.log: The Consort laughs, shortly. 'Don't,' they say. 'Wait.' You hear it as advice and then as a confession.

events.text: {npc} tests you. The test is petty and exact: a cup left on the wrong table, a quiet remark about your cooking, a door left ajar at the wrong hour. Each one is a small flag of defiance, planted in the household like a pin in a map. By the end of the month you can read the map.

choices.text: Ignore each pin, and never mention them

effects.log: You say nothing. By the second month {npc} has run out of pins, and starts leaving the doors closed on purpose. It is the beginning of a truce.

choices.text: Answer each pin with a small, kind courtesy

effects.log: A cup, returned, with a flower in it. A cooked dish, adjusted to taste. {npc} is baffled, and then furious, and then, by degrees, quiet.

choices.text: Confront {him} with the map

effects.log: You lay the pins out one by one. {npc} reddens. 'What do you want?' {he} says. 'For you to be unhappy honestly,' you say, 'not by way of the teacup.'

events.text: The household's old gardener, a minor god of ferns, tells you that {npc} sits at night in the garden, near the pond, and speaks to the water. You go out in the dark and stand at a polite distance. {He} is describing, in a low voice, the funeral of the parent's old house. It was, it seems, a quiet affair.

choices.text: Sit down beside {him} and listen

mem.note: listened to me by the pond

effects.log: You sit on the cold stone and listen. {npc} does not stop talking. By dawn, {he} has described all of it, the colours of the banners, the smell of the incense, the last word said by an uncle. It is a good funeral, told right.

choices.text: Leave a lantern by the pond and go

effects.log: You leave the lantern, lit, on the stone. In the morning it is still there, still lit, and a cup of tea has been left next to it, cold, for you.

events.text: At the end of the season, {npc} is called home to the Lineage. {He} stands in the hall with the travelling-case in {his} hand, the same case, and it is obvious that {he} has something to say and has been rehearsing it badly. 'The address,' {he} says at last, 'was not as wrong as I thought.'

choices.text: Tell {him} the door stays open

mem.note: told me the door stayed open

effects.log: {npc} nods, gravely. 'Yes,' {he} says. 'I know.' {He} goes. Twice that year a crane lands on your sill with a pressed fern and no note, and you hang them both on the wall.

choices.text: Ask {him} to come back at the next festival

mem.note: asked me back for the festival

effects.log: {npc} agrees, with a look that suggests this was the right thing to ask. The next festival brings a different {npc}, calmer, and with a gift.

events.text: {npc} and the twin, Dami, born a heartbeat apart, have each been tested by the Court's registrar and each found to bear a spark of the very same domain. The Book of Fates has one page for one heir. The two are very polite about it at table, and watch each other's hands.

choices.text: Divide the domain between the two of them

effects.log: You propose a division: one the gathering half, one the giving. The Court looks sceptical. The twins look at each other, and for the first time in a month, speak.

choices.text: Name {npc} as the heir, by right of the first breath

effects.log: You name {npc}. The Court records it. Dami nods, once, and leaves the room, and is not seen at table for a week.

choices.text: Name neither, and ask them to decide

effects.log: You ask them to decide. They look at each other with identical suspicion. 'Fine,' says Dami. 'A contest.' They go out. The hall waits.

events.text: The twins' first contest is a simple one: a cloud, shaped by the domain, over the courtyard. {npc} builds a tower. Dami builds a boat. The cloud-tower and the cloud-boat float side by side for a moment, and the household holds its breath as one trembles and tips toward the other.

choices.text: Catch the boat before it hits the tower

effects.log: You catch the boat in a net of your own domain. The twins stare at you, then at one another. 'We were fine,' Dami mutters. They were not, quite, and both know it.

choices.text: Let the boat and tower collide

effects.log: They collide, and the cloud collapses into a shower. The twins, drenched, begin to laugh, simultaneously, helplessly, and the contest is called off by mutual absurdity.

choices.text: Declare the contest a draw before it ends

effects.log: You declare it, in a clear voice. The twins turn on you in perfect unison. 'We hadn't finished,' they say. You see that you have united them against yourself.

events.text: Dami comes to you alone one evening, with a quiet face. 'I think {npc} should have the page,' Dami says. 'I will go to a mortal world and keep a shrine of my own. I do not need a Book. But I would like to be asked, before I am sent away.' There is something very sad and very proud in the offer.

choices.text: Refuse the offer and keep both of them near

effects.log: 'No one is going anywhere,' you say. Dami looks startled, then furious, then, finally, relieved. The Book will find a way to hold two, you decide, or the Book will have to change.

choices.text: Accept, and help Dami find a shrine worth keeping

effects.log: You and Dami spend a season finding a shrine. It is a small hillside spring in a world of rice and rain. Dami is quiet at the leaving, and then, at the last, waves.

events.text: The Book of Fates, surprisingly, accommodates the sharing. Registrar Ilhyeon, on discovering that nothing in the Book forbids two heirs to a single domain, spends a week in the library. At the end of it Ilhyeon writes a two-line footnote that makes {npc} and Dami, for the first time, a single entry in the Book.

choices.text: Frame the footnote and hang it in the hall

effects.log: The footnote is framed in dark wood. The twins, passing, each touch the frame, and each pretends not to have. It becomes a household custom.

choices.text: Thank Ilhyeon with a private gift

effects.log: Ilhyeon, startled, accepts. The next visit comes with a basket of plums and a long, awkward silence. The Registrar has made a friend, and finds it disquieting.
